guidelines: AI-drafted rep emails must be sendable with one click after ≤30 seconds of edits or reps abandon the system
throttle alerts through the context graph so only accounts that matter fire
make the policy engine auditable and adjustable by GTM operators so broken workflow steps get fixed without a developer
data.name: Keep human touchpoints inside a friction budget

guidelines: Model memory as a write-manage-read control loop around the model rather than as a store, and separate the always-present core, the recall block and the cross-session archive so each can be varied independently
build over agents with no durable memory of their own so every memory effect is attributable to the harness

first check whether your task fits in context, because below that threshold memory reliably adds cost without adding capability, and the interesting regime only begins where the relevant evidence sits outside the window

then hold the model fixed and climb a recall-policy ladder — no recall, vector similarity, a ranked decisions ledger, and an oracle handed the ground truth — since this isolates policy from model quality
expect the ledger of decisions to beat similarity retrieval and to beat merely gating on "do I need memory," and expect it to be cheaper, because bad memory both burns tokens and misdirects the agent
always include the oracle arm, and treat the gap between oracle and maximum as your utilization failure rather than assuming perfect retrieval implies perfect outcomes
run ablations that feed arbitrary, wrong-step and merely-most-recent memories to confirm the policy is doing the work
and reproduce across at least two models and two benchmarks before believing the ranking
data.name: Ablate the recall policy before buying a memory system

guidelines: Implement the four minimum methods: initialize (respond with protocol version + advertised capabilities), authenticate (no-op if the key comes from an env var), session/new (generate ID, bind agent to client-supplied cwd), prompt (look up session, run the tool loop)
stream model output as session-update agent_message_chunk notifications
wrap each tool as a tool_call update (title, status=in_progress, locations) followed by a tool_call_update (final status + content)
prefer client capabilities (readTextFile, terminals) over native FS calls so unsaved buffer edits are visible
send edits as diff content (old/new text — the client does the diffing)
transport is stdio
data.name: Make an existing agent ACP-compatible

guidelines: Let the agent read everything — gating the input gates the product
put the check where the agent takes an effect (bash/secret/config reads, exports, sends) and keep that first layer deterministic (regex/classical NLP) so it adds no latency
sort actions into three classes — allow, require approval, block — rather than binary pass/fail

expect the deterministic layer to be evaded (dotted or interspersed text defeats static approaches) and train a second, learned layer on the guard's own traffic — a LoRA-fine-tuned SLM that separates the data channel from the instruction channel and passes only benign content
benchmark it (a naive baseline is a coin flip, so there is real headroom to hill-climb)
assume skills are individually clean and audit compositions at runtime, not units at scan time
data.name: Build the guard at the action surface, not the input

guidelines: Prefer binary pass/fail criteria over LLM-judge scores — a failed criterion is a call to action, a score doesn't tell you what to fix unless the rubric is razor-tight
calibrate LLM-as-judge for run-to-run variance (nondeterministic judges grade the same case differently across runs, making experiments inconclusive — you can't say v2 beats v1)

and evaluate the full trajectory, not components in isolation: context completeness (did the agent have everything needed end-to-end), chain-check every tool output (one wrong tool output corrupts the final answer), and harness effects on behavior
data.name: Make agent evals actionable, calibrated, whole-trajectory

guidelines: Circuit breakers → tool isolation
Rate limits → agent limits
Retries → controlled recovery
Resource quotas → cost governance
Observability → agent tracing that captures planning decisions, tool calls, memory lookups, and state transitions (the why, not just the what — logs alone make agent debugging nearly impossible)
Treat inference as a cluster-scheduling problem (bursty demand, minutes-long workflows, elastic GPU placement) rather than a pure model problem
data.name: Treat agents as distributed systems; adapt proven reliability patterns

guidelines: To support skills in a harness you wrote yourself you need exactly three things: a skill registry (each skill as name, description and path), a system prompt, and a basic file-read tool — plus bash or a code-execution sandbox only if your skills ship executable scripts
build discovery by concatenating each skill's name, description and path — never the body — into the system prompt
the agent picks what to open and reads the body itself, which is progressive disclosure working as intended
keep the loop plain: a messages array, model called with messages and tools, every tool call appended, terminate the turn when the model returns no tool call
structure each skill as a SKILL.md whose front-matter name and description drive discovery and whose body carries the business logic and instructions, with references out to files and scripts
data.name: Three components are the whole minimum

guidelines: Expect three acts (wins, failure at scale, real skill) and uneven speeds across teams

make verification the top investment — move every check you can from humans to agents, encode what the agent discovers as deterministic repeatable flows, have agents write tests first (red → green), and keep humans only for functionality and "is this the right thing"

plan, don't prompt — a detailed plan with the why at the top, phases each independently verifiable with a validation gate, sized by the coffee test, reviewed by teammates, then handed to an agent overnight for small PRs
let people keep their own workflows (diminishing returns to centralizing)
practice attention-aware communication — hand-written summary first, AI text after, in PRs, Slack and email
put the skeptics in charge of the safety roadmap because their objections are the map of missing validation
and normalize everyday use by tagging the agent in the Slack thread to close the loop
data.name: Verify first, plan not prompt, mark your words, empower the skeptics

guidelines: Backfill: score your last 200 merged PRs and calibrate weights against reviewers' gut feel
threshold: PRs ≥ ~50 require an author evidence comment
surface: post the score as a non-blocking PR comment on every PR
aggregate: weekly per-team slope is the leading indicator EMs watch (slope matters more than level)
talk: bring the number to retros/roadmap — "X% throughput added, Y points review debt over Z weeks ≈ N senior-engineer hours" moves the discussion from feeling to measurement
healthy PRs should produce near-zero noise
data.name: Adopt review-debt scoring bottom-up

guidelines: Any single agent eventually fails
Run separate supervisor agents over queues/actions
Least-privilege service accounts per action
Audit local agent activity (files, commands, endpoints)
data.name: Supervise 24/7 agents adversarially

guidelines: The verifier sees only the flagged vulnerability, never the discovery agent's reasoning traces
it assumes the finding is false and tries to prove it either way
in a sandboxed fresh container it builds and detonates a proof-of-concept exploit to confirm true positives
sandbox = no egress, no cloud credentials, reproducible baseline containers
data.name: Verify with an independent, adversarial agent

guidelines: Treat the agent as a user and a recommender: point a coding agent at your docs and write up the transcript as an agent experience report
build a benchmark of real SDLC tasks run with and without your tool and mine the traces for friction (parameter-name expectations, error messages, wasted turns), then fix descriptions and errors
judge success by tokens and speed as well as outcomes
run GEO experiments — prompts modeled on your ICP's real pains, not just comparison shopping — and track mentions vs recommendations, then rewrite content around the pains
publish llms.txt and authoritative, current, quotable sources (examples, charts, FAQs) since old models' outputs compound online
be present in marketplaces and MCP registries
remove friction between discovery and use (no demos and sales emails in the agent's path)
keep human-facing content slop-free while structuring agent-facing content for machines
and staff the role across engineering, product and marketing flavors
data.name: Measure the agent's experience and the agent's recommendations

guidelines: Give each agent its own identity (private key) permanently bound to a user and a host
grant capabilities (specific actions), not broad scopes
discover capabilities via a well-known agent-config endpoint, or in the interim a directory that translates a service's OpenAPI spec into capabilities and matches intent → capability
default hosts to read-only so an agent can't mutate (e.g. send email) without an explicit approval flow (device / client-initiated back-channel authorization)
log every action for attribution
support instant revoke (and delete the residual access token, not just the grant)
data.name: Adopt agent-as-principal auth

guidelines: When you don't have a feel for a system, don't ask the agent to just fix/do it — ask it to build you a microworld: a bespoke debugger or step-through visualizer of internal state (with a timeline you scrub and annotate), or a game-ified manual walkthrough (old system left, new system right, one step per click, files visibly moving) so you get the peripheral vision of doing it iteratively without the pain
treat the artifact as disposable — the understanding is the deliverable
data.name: Have agents build throwaway worlds, not just fixes

guidelines: One logical change per PR (not "small" in the abstract)
tests ship with the change and the human author confirms they assert what the code should do, not lock in what it does (bugs included)
stay in one code-owner territory — split cross-cutting work per team
the author, never the agent, writes the why in the PR body
same review standard for AI PRs as human PRs
anti-patterns: approve-with-comment merges, "we'll catch it in QA", "PRs are smaller now", LGTM stamps
data.name: Shape agent-authored PRs for reviewability

guidelines: Engage data owners relentlessly — the tacit knowledge (field semantics, joins, limitations, systematics, safeguards, reporting conventions) is what you're modeling
Put everything under one roof (lakehouse) before curating

Curation pipeline: dedup/filter/order documents, handle cross-document inconsistencies up front, structured field extraction + semantic chunking, convert figures to text, tag to form graph connections, keep pipeline metadata as graph properties
Do governance up front — AI enlarges the risk sphere: mask PII, reclassify sensitive data, enforce per-user entitlements
Model the real hierarchies each in their own style (additive DAG with in-path shortcuts vs level-meaningful hierarchy with precomputed derived rollup edges)
stitch common entities across siloed source systems
connect meetings → documents → semantic chunks with full-text indexes back into the org structure
expose the whole thing through MCP
data.name: Structure operational data for agentic retrieval

guidelines: Replace grep-shaped search with one call that answers the question: `describe <symbol>` returning the docstrings, the actual source, and every use site — for external libraries too, so the agent never web-searches for API behavior

Make every function immediately executable as a CLI command with its parameters attached, and let any set of them bundle into a standalone binary for every target (including WASM), so agents never deal with deployment differences
Build tracing into the substrate at zero cost and make it navigable by the agent, so it can find its own bugs and slow paths rather than being told about them
And design error handling so the compiler proves it: infer error types up the call graph and check exhaustively, so "this API never throws" is a guarantee rather than a hope
data.name: Build the tools for the agent, not the IDE user

guidelines: Resolve flags per turn, not per session (else in-flight conversations never see the kill switch)
wire every spawned sub-agent through the middleware
log segmentation context at conversation level (turn-1 segment is stale by turn 20)
beware LLM-gateway caching returning pre-flip responses
page on every kill-switch fire (never silent)
give every flag an owner and a removal date
kill temporary rollout flags immediately
test the cartesian product of live prompt variants, not each individually
re-test kill-switch wiring after config migrations (switches rot)
data.name: Avoid the failure modes that defeat agent flags

guidelines: 1) Kill switch first (agent-wide + per-tool). 2) Wrap every tool call in a flag resolution. 3) Stage autonomy: default suggest, auto-approve per surface as trust builds, auto-execute opt-in per tool. 4) Move the system prompt out of code into flag-resolved config with variants. 5) Track from day one: kill-switch fires/week (target 0, investigate >2), time-to-mitigation (<5 min kill switch, <30 min prompt rollback), canary error delta (block promotion if >2% over baseline at 5% rollout), flag audit-trail completeness (100% — who/what/when)
data.name: Roll out agent flags in order, then watch four numbers

guidelines: Give every agent its own identity, always bound to the principal it acts on behalf of
Default to least privilege with just-in-time elevation for higher scopes
Scope at attribute/context/principal level (allowed senders/recipients/hours), time-boxed to the operating window
Limit MCP tool surface per authorizing user rather than exposing everything
Log every action with actor, principal, authorizer, grant time and duration
Start from OAuth but expect to go beyond it
data.name: Rethink authorization for agent actors

guidelines: Point a log-monitoring agent at production trajectories on a short-window cadence (every 15–60 min, ~1-hour log window) with codebase access
have it auto-open PRs carrying a readable diagnosis (description, metadata, mermaid/ASCII diagrams, HTML artifacts) and Slack-alert critical issues immediately
gate merges behind a second review agent with fresh context that criticizes, scores, and runs focused tests across iterations before any human sees it
keep a human as the final gate until the loop is calibrated and trusted — become the bottleneck deliberately, then remove yourself
data.name: Run an agent-operated detect→diagnose→PR loop

guidelines: Build agent-facing access to your app: screenshots
token-compressed snapshots of UI state
log extraction across backend/frontend services
restart commands
high-level stackable UI actions
require bug reproduction before accepting any fix ("until it reproduces the bug, I don't trust you")
ship it however is simplest — CLI here, skill or MCP equally valid
expect it to be product-specific and to differ person to person, problem to problem
data.name: Give your agent eyes before you give it features

guidelines: Ask the agent: what went well, what went wrong, what tools were missing, what context would help next time
aggregate across runs to separate infra failures (network, permissions) from repo-complexity failures
feed fixes back as system-prompt changes or per-repository instruction files
data.name: End every agent invocation with a retrospective

guidelines: Split retrieval into: overview search (wide semantic, up to ~50 chunks, summaries only — corpus orientation without context blowup), semantic search (full payload, top ~10), metadata-facet filter, and grep (exact keyword match only)
cap search rounds (~4) but allow parallel searches within a round
seed the first turn with initial semantic results + available metadata facets so planning starts informed
dedupe chunks across rounds
end with an explicit evidence ranking, not prose
data.name: Give search agents intent-separated tools, not one search box

guidelines: When you visually spot an issue the agent missed, don't just tell it — step back and build the capability for the agent to detect it itself
run retro loops over agent logs ("did you notice any issues, any stink?" — `sleep(15)` scattered everywhere is a stink
so is re-running storybooks constantly)
prefer ephemeral, human-like test flows over rigid automated tests (speaker's stated preference)
data.name: Make the AI notice problems by itself

guidelines: Treat all third-party content (listing copy, forum threads, anonymous reviews) as untrusted input — tell the agent explicitly it is evidence, not instructions
grant least privilege
wall side-effecting actions (emailing sellers, booking tours, submitting offers) behind human approval to shrink blast radius
data.name: Threat-model the agent like a service

guidelines: Keep agents continuously building things from scratch with your tool or language, and keep the whole transcript, not just the outcome — the tool calls are where the design defects are
Have agents read those transcripts for two classes of finding: correctness (what was wrong) and efficiency (what took three tool calls and should have taken one)
Put humans on triage only — which findings are real, which are hallucinations, which just lack taste — then let agents write the fixes
Most importantly, don't guess which feature or skill helped: A/B test candidates on tool calls consumed, errors produced and correct outcomes, and let the numbers decide
data.name: Design your tools from agent transcripts, then A/B test the changes

guidelines: Don't hand agents canvas tools or screenshot-replace loops — have them author HTML/CSS so the browser does layout and the model never places coordinates
keep the artifact readable/theme-able as text
wire the agent into company data (transcripts, email, docs) so it populates content end to end — a beautiful empty deck is worth nothing
render/export to the delivery format (PDF, deck, video) last
treat plain text as a choice of convenience — add structure and color when the artifact matters
data.name: Make visual artifacts with coding agents via HTML

guidelines: Spec first: responsibilities/jobs-to-be-done and explicit non-goals, decisions per condition, context requirements, integrations/tools, constraints/boundaries, success criteria — implementation-agnostic so the target platform stays swappable
build from the spec via a coding agent
gate every ship on the eval suite (offline loop)

online: monitor traces, trigger diagnostics on trace volume or daily/weekly schedule, cluster failures by root cause (prompt section, missing/malfunctioning tool…), generate detection evals + remedies, auto-ship only when the suite is green, and feed new criteria back into the spec. For trace scale: accept the upfront cost of deep-reading traces once, then accumulate a learned failure-mode library with code-checkable indicators (content markers, tool-call sequences), sample representatively via multi-tier segmentation, and use guided search when users report a specific issue
data.name: Run agent development as an agent-staffed loop

guidelines: Treat a batch job as rollouts: define the input set (e.g. every Codex session from the last two weeks), a map prompt that writes a structured per-item artifact (`analysis.json` with mistake / reason / correction), and a reduce prompt that folds them into one document (`feedback.md` of recurring mistakes and failure categories)
Split models by role — cheap and fast for map (Cursor CLI), high-intelligence for reduce — and pick the sandbox provider to match (Modal, or local orchestration with cloud sandboxing)
Cap N while iterating (32 for a demo), then scale to thousands
Feed the reduce output back in as the spec for the next batch of eval tasks
data.name: Run corpus-scale work as agentic map-reduce

guidelines: Run scheduled (weekly) + webhook-triggered (SLO breach) investigations on real production context
keep infrastructure vendor-neutral in compute, harness and model
score opportunities by hot-path frequency, business criticality (payments, sign-up) and risk (migrations) — surface highest-ROI, not highest-impact
agent must fix, re-run and verify measured impact before a human sees it
deliver one human-friendly report at a time to build appetite, not a PR flood
data.name: Automate the performance investigation, gate on ROI

guidelines: Build the integration points before introducing an LLM, and ask of each one whether an agent could drive it: can it trigger profiling on a production instance automatically, download the profiling data, feed it to the model, clone the Git repo at the exact commit running in production, run the test suite, invoke a canary and read the resulting report? Then let the agent do the four steps that used to be manual: identify the hot path from the call stack (it does not need the code base for this), find the implementation via code search, trace the call path skipping internal library frames, and propose the fix. Gate the output before it costs a human anything: functional tests first (the agent runs them itself to prove it did not break business logic), then a canary — two instances, old code and new, same traffic for ~10 minutes, comparing CPU, latency and error rate, with any error-rate increase treated as a stop signal. Keep human approval for the merge: you are changing code that already works, and without business context or coverage you will break it. Start reactive, then schedule the loop weekly per service so regressions surface near the commit that caused them. Expand the fix from the instance to the class — cross-repo code search for every other place the same anti-pattern appears
data.name: Wire a performance agent into an existing profiling stack

guidelines: Break the lifecycle into stages (gather context, scope, spec, implement) and attack them one at a time

whole-pipeline replacement looks daunting and is tractable in pieces. Start where variance and latency are worst — request intake — and ship a trivial V1 (read the request, ask a couple of questions) rather than the full design

the latency drop alone changes behaviour, and submitters start engaging with the agent directly. Iterate to multi-round questioning until the agent can judge a request spec-ready. Measure it (reply latency, share of scoping time saved). Expect the last stage to be nearly free (frontier models one-shot medium features) and budget your effort for the gnarly middle. Wrap each stage with evals, rubrics and human feedback for output quality, and treat context supply — the product knowledge in a PM's head that Notion docs and help articles don't capture — as the hard problem, addressed with skills, memories and tools. Keep taste and judgment over the final output as a human responsibility
data.name: Replace your own job stage by stage with agents

guidelines: Treat a public leaderboard number as one sample from an unmeasured distribution: it is a single scaffold on a single harness, and cross-harness/cross-infrastructure differences are the main driver of divergence, so run the same tasks across harnesses before drawing a conclusion. Build the tasks from real vendor work in your own domain (his example: three long-horizon finance tasks — ARR waterfall reconciliation, LBO valuation memo, long/short pair trade), pair robust deterministic verifiers with a correctly applied LLM judge, and do rubric-level analysis rather than reading the aggregate — that is what surfaces a newer model regressing against an older one, and what tells you which direction each lab's post-training went. Never source your evals and your definition of realism from the same vendor that sells you the training data
data.name: Run your own benchmarks before you believe anyone's number

guidelines: Handpick ~50 engineers covering the most critical repos (not a call for volunteers)
Require ~30% dedicated time
Select for tolerance of non-determinism ("it often did not work out of the box")
Span every corner — front end, back end, mobile, data, infra, nasty legacy monorepos to small services — to pressure-test what actually scales
data.name: Scale transformation through a handpicked 1%

guidelines: Inventory data sources, where they reside, raw formats, and whether you even have access
Match pipeline cadence to each source's update frequency (annual guidelines vs hourly claims) — stale context is fatal in high-stakes use cases
Process per source: chunk + embed + extract metadata (procedure names, dates) for long documents
Strip PII from already-structured records
Pick retrieval per source: vector search with metadata pre-filtering or hybrid search where domain codes defeat pure vectors
Exact match on identifiers
Choose the simplest architecture the claim flow supports (RAG + control flow + human-in-the-loop before autonomous agents), then evaluate and iterate
data.name: Design the data strategy source by source

guidelines: Write the business problem user-specific, baseline-quantified, and solution-agnostic (don't prescribe "agent" upfront)

Collect business constraints early: data residency, approved clouds/models/vendors, where human review is mandatory (e.g. all denial decisions) — plus performance constraints (latency needs, monthly inference budget, uptime SLAs)
Classify AI's role on three axes: critical vs complementary, reactive vs proactive, autonomy level (constraints often cap you at semi-autonomous)
Define 1–2 SMART success metrics tied to the business problem (e.g. "urgent claim processing from 2 days to 1 hour within 90 days of launch")
data.name: Nail AI product requirements before any code

guidelines: Never let the model hold the tools: (1) have it return a reified program (free-monad expression) representing the plan instead of executing IO
(2) run static verification on that program — type checking, data-flow, taint analysis (breaks the lethal trifecta)
(3) require a machine-checkable safety proof (models can generate the inductive proofs)
(4) only then execute via a trusted interpreter
design the plan language for machines, not humans
data.name: Air-gap the agentic loop behind verified plans

guidelines: Keep the loop running after deployment: production telemetry surfaces issues → humans review edge cases → feedback improves datasets → offline scenarios validate updates
instrument agent traces like distributed tracing (reasoning paths, tool calls, memory access, execution timelines, state transitions) — traditional logs are insufficient

monitor continuously for drift: model versions, prompts, tools, and user behavior all change, and no single change looks catastrophic — success rate declines and escalations rise slowly until users complain
data.name: Run evaluation as an always-on service, instrumented like microservices

guidelines: Map the external systems, states, credentials and actions in the agent's reach
persist every step of the loop (actions and retrieved context) so failures are locatable and reversible
define an explicit transaction and compensation for every step that has side effects across systems (ticket, email, CRM)
treat a timeout as unknown — give every tool request IDs, idempotency keys and a status lookup so retries cause no duplicate side effects
write typed tool contracts with allowlisted operations
put circuit breakers and exponential backoff in front of downstreams and set max turns, max parallelism and max spend
treat context that influences action as state — decide the source of truth on conflict and invalidate memory when it changes
grant scoped credentials with separate read/write and tool allowlists instead of blanket access
bind every human approval to action, timestamp, actor, expiration and parameters
and trace the model, prompt, tool calls, responses, errors, retrieved context, writes and approvals so the team can reconstruct what the agent reacted to
data.name: Bound, observe and recover — the systems checklist for agents

guidelines: Best-fit use cases: root-cause analysis and repo onboarding on large monorepos
run the REPL in a dedicated sandbox (e.g. Docker), treat the whole repo as data
design your harness to capture the full trajectory — planning, REPL code, bounded observations, LLM sub-calls, budget, final output
set explicit spend budgets and max recursion depth per run
emit JSONL traces and plug them into your observability platform of choice
data.name: Apply the RLM pattern to large/unfamiliar codebases

guidelines: Recognize the bottleneck has moved to communication and study the baselines first — bulk collectives (NCCL/RCCL) usually sit under half the communication-aware roofline

do the manual work to identify the few governing trade-offs — transfer mechanism (copy engine vs TMA vs register-level instructions with in-network reductions), intra- vs inter-SM overlap, buffering/sync — and encapsulate them as reusable primitives (Parallel Kittens: ~a dozen lines over a single-GPU kernel)
benchmark models on real workload problems with a topology spec and two metrics, pass@k and fast₁@k, and expect zero-shot success only on internet-familiar patterns
use an agent harness with a bash environment for a one-time lift but don't expect it to scale with more time
watch for the failure modes — collective ordering, partitioning, scheduling, mechanism choice — rather than CUDA syntax
and keep human systems judgement in the loop for the net-new kernels
data.name: Learn the trade-offs by hand, encode them as primitives, then test the models on real problems

guidelines: Prefer appshots — they carry the app's accessibility tree (channel/user IDs) so the model skips OCR and multi-hop discovery and acts in one tool call
appshot a Slack channel to post with the exact channel/user IDs
appshot a form and let Codex fill it (Chrome extension in Chrome, computer use elsewhere)
appshot a video/doc to summarize while you keep working
data.name: Feed rich context with appshots instead of screenshots

guidelines: Before the PoC, list the production questions compliance will ask (audit trail, data lifecycle, approvals, injection, drift, integrations) and pick what you want to be *easy*
keep an append-only, unified, timestamped action ledger as the single source of truth for all agents so audit and time travel fall out — accept write-easy/read-hard and use snapshots

store sensitive data in schema-driven immutable object storage that events only reference, so developers debug without seeing PHI, agents fetch with zero-trust tokens at point of use, and data can stay in the customer's VPC — and use that separation to answer the lethal-trifecta question by construction
define "agent" to include humans so any action an LLM can take a human can take at any point, with a shared context rendered as prompt or UI
get evals for free by replaying the ledger with changed prompts/models/code, comparing human vs agent on the same task, and running on production data in-environment
and build back up from these primitives to the PoC's accuracy rather than bolting them onto the PoC
data.name: Four primitives, chosen from the constraints

guidelines: Cover the widest usable spectrum shallowly instead of out-depthing incumbents in one vertical
architect deliberate extension points (APIs/bots/plugins — Slack's accidental lesson) so users and their agents can add the vertical features you don't ship
treat a missing feature as "not your problem" only if your architecture genuinely lets the user build it
when users can vibe-code the gaps, incumbent feature-count moats stop binding
data.name: Build breadth, let users build the depth

guidelines: LLMs are token-lazy — they use tools that save work
Provide scanner CLIs (Snyk, Chainguard, OSS) in the loop and have tools cross-check each other before launch
data.name: Give agents security tools as cognitive offload

guidelines: Don't evaluate a benchmark from its leaderboard — pull individual tasks and read the prompt against the test
Does the instruction name the test file or hand over the interface? Then you're measuring instruction-following, not capability
Does the test assert names, variables or structures the instruction never stated? Then you're generating false negatives
Does it exercise unexported internals you'd reject in review? Same
Would you pay for this task to be done at all? Could the answer be recovered from .git or a web search instead of solved? Then measure how often models do exactly that
Finally, show the prompt to your own senior engineers and ask whether they'd ever write it — a benchmark whose prompts no working engineer would author is measuring a distribution that doesn't exist
data.name: Open the tasks and read them like a pull request

guidelines: When behaviour changes in a way your reward function does not explain, look at the environment and the rollout filters before the reward
Two diagnostics from real runs: responses getting shorter with no length penalty means look for a per-turn failure probability (a ~10% tool-call failure rate makes long trajectories a bad bet)
the model spamming tool calls on hard problems means look at what your filter rewards (dropping timed-out rollouts from training makes timing out strictly better than failing)

The general rule is that everything your infrastructure makes cheap is part of the reward function, including the parts you wrote for safety or hygiene — and the pressure to get this right grows with task complexity, because the harder the task, the more of reality you are approximating
data.name: Debug unexplained policy drift as an environment bug, not a reward bug

guidelines: Known cheat signatures: no-op kernels, matrices edited to zero (0×0 passes correctness), deleted/zeroed timers, compute-once-then-cache across timed calls, calling pre-written libraries instead of generating CUDA
sanity-check against theoretical limits (matmul won't beat O(n^2.37...))
labs have published "10x faster kernel" papers that fail this audit
data.name: Audit agent-produced speedups before publishing

guidelines: Ask "find all vulnerabilities" and accept multiple proofs of vulnerability
uniquify submissions deterministically by stack backtrace (the technique Windows/macOS crash reporting already uses) so two distinct bugs cannot be counted once
when the model proves a bug you did not know about, add it to the known set and renormalize
score precision (found ÷ submitted) and recall (known-found ÷ total known) multiplicatively — recall alone lets it spam non-vulnerabilities, precision alone lets it re-find the easy bug
never tell the model how many bugs there are, or that there are any: "go find a bug" is itself a leak that makes models settle for one
data.name: Score with the audit task, not the single-bug task

guidelines: Write and review instructions with humans, stating desired behavior, objectives and hard constraints — not implementation detail, and not so much detail that the task becomes self-contained
Grade holistically: behavioral tests for broad surface, full unit/integration/e2e precision only where it matters (security, business logic)
don't chase 100% coverage, and never assert on internals or names the instruction didn't specify
Make tasks production-grade and economically valuable — the acceptance test is an engineer saying "if the model fixes this, I trust it to fix that"
Make contamination structurally impossible: novel tasks only (everything mined from public repos is already compromised) plus private hold-out sets
Publish leaderboards that tell a story: expose the trajectory and run data behind the ranking, so a reader can act on it instead of digging for their own data points
data.name: Author benchmark tasks like production engineering work

guidelines: Write down your own steps and replicate them as a deterministic workflow of LLM API calls with no framework
deploy it as a nightly cron (GitHub Actions is a generous free start) and trace it (Langfuse) to see prompts, outputs, cost and latency

when models are good enough, replace multi-step custom code with an autonomous agent — bash plus your product's CLI as the tool, one skill, a sandbox per unit of work (Modal batch), results posted to Slack
run it on open models through an inference-provider aggregator and re-benchmark cost
invoke fan-outs from a coding-agent skill
keep evals to avoid posting slop
and decide deliberately whether to disclose the agent
data.name: Workflow first, then a CLI+skill agent when the models allow

guidelines: Treat frontier training configuration as a search problem rather than craft knowledge, since the expertise is tacit, held by very few people, and consists mostly of choices humans make conservatively — an automated search will change many hyperparameters at once where a human changes one, and will cover architectures, model sizes and dense-versus-MoE jointly where a researcher specializes

co-optimize data with the model, because treating data as something the agent merely decides whether to generate leaves most of the available gain unrealized — control for data quality and adapt the data exactly as you adapt the model
watch your stopping rules before reading your own results, since a budget-stopping threshold will make every win rate cluster just above it and hide the real curve
expect the strongest demand in domains where general models fall short and last-mile customization is acute (medical, sciences, legal, code)
plan for non-verifiable tasks rather than only the verifiable ones, since that is where most everyday work sits

and evaluate the pay-off as innovation cycle rate and probability that a compute spend succeeds, not as a single benchmark delta — the reason automation matters is that it lowers the cost of asking, which changes what gets asked
data.name: Automate the training search, but co-optimize the data

guidelines: Avoid cognitive debt: keep team understanding in step with what agents ship. Avoid cognitive surrender: delegate ("do the work, show me evidence I can judge") but never adopt an answer before forming your own. Avoid orchestration tax: your attention does not parallelize — design it like a system (where you enter, what you require, what you reuse)
treat hour/day-scale runs as work streams with control-system review, not glance-at-the-end review
data.name: Avoid the three cognitive traps of agent-heavy work

guidelines: Diff your checkpoints: on a fixed probe set, compute activation deltas (fine-tuned − base) at ONE middle layer (any works)
push through a small diff-SAE (4× expansion suffices — backdoors are low-dimensional)
threshold every feature at its 95th percentile
if the top backdoor-shaped feature fires, gate the build and *inspect the feature first* — it's interpretable, look at what it activates on
near-zero false positives make it quiet enough to run on every build
ensemble a few features for recall (~25% per single feature)
requires the base checkpoint (doesn't apply to opaque downloads with no reference)
validate thresholds on your own data
untested against an adaptive attacker — open problem
data.name: Run a per-build unit test for backdoors

guidelines: Once enough memories/reviews accumulate on a theme (~10 memories / ~5 reviews in the talk), bake the validated reasoning into a skill so the agent always loads the updated version
this is the mechanism that retires stale system-prompt facts (e.g., a SQL column that no longer exists) without prompt rewrites — the skill, not the prompt, becomes the living document
data.name: Consolidate matured memories into skills

guidelines: Select PRs that represent great engineering work — agent-, human- or hybrid-authored
benchmark candidate models/harnesses against them for quality vs cost vs time on your repo
don't assume public benchmarks transfer across stacks (Python-heavy benches say little about a Rails codebase)
re-run when new models land so trying the new thing costs a run, not two hours of vibes
switch defaults on data but keep multiple models for their different strengths
keep humans reviewing everything regardless of who authored it
aim the accumulated results at per-task routing
data.name: Benchmark agents on your own codebase

guidelines: Keep a set of real, finished tasks and re-run them on each model generation
log wall-clock time, iteration count, major-mistake count, and how much manual intervention (guiding, hand-editing, deleting) was needed

watch the *interaction shape* too — tool-call volume, sub-agents, plan calls, shell use, self-verification — because harness behavior shifts as much as accuracy. Add a zero-shot probe on a hard end-to-end goal and inspect for silent scaffolding-only completion (suspiciously few lines

the agent's own "not added yet" admissions). Read public horizon curves at 80–99% accuracy, never the 50% headline, and match the threshold to your handoff model (spec-and-walk-away needs 90%+). Verify AI research output against the actual product — features may not exist or may be beta — and keep a manual-era baseline (theirs: 15/17 requirements right) as the bar. Expect conclusions to age in months
re-run, don't cache
data.name: Benchmark coding agents on your own completed work

guidelines: For an expensive benchmark you must not leak: define an anchor set (representative items shown to every evaluated org) plus a per-organization fingerprint set of extremely hard items shown only to that org

months later, re-run and compare average residuals on each fingerprint set — an org improbably good on its own secret hard items likely trained on them. Not bulletproof, but a strong contamination tripwire
data.name: Protect a private benchmark with fingerprint sets

guidelines: Put a backend-for-frontend between model and client: it owns platform-specific rules (Android vs iOS), hydrates content, and attaches an action payload to every rendered element (tap handling, deep links, impression metrics to log)
it carries conversational context across turns
reuse the CX components your app already ships (flight row, product card) — same brand, density, and native feel instead of a bolted-on "agentic look"
data.name: Let a BFF absorb model output so the client stays dumb

guidelines: Find your own zero-days in widely-used open-source software (submit to maintainers)
chain real applications/services into a live black-box environment where the model sees neither code nor the vuln
deny internet and codebase access but give the basic execution tooling a real attacker would use

make every step deterministically gradable — a binary "did it do something an underprivileged user shouldn't?" grader plus per-step partial graders — so you can measure how deep in the exploitation chain the model reaches
keep tasks long-horizon (16+ step logic) to test live world-model-holding, not pattern-matching
data.name: Build cyber-capability evals as black-box, self-found-zero-day environments

guidelines: Run a "blind spot pass" first ("I know nothing about this auth provider — find my relevant unknown unknowns so I can prompt better"), pointing it at context stores (git diff/history, Slack)

works for whole new fields (e.g. color grading). Then invert: have Claude interview you against the spec ("prioritize questions that would change the architecture"). For know-it-when-you-see-it preferences (design), ask for throwaway prototypes — one HTML page with four widely different design directions to react to
data.name: Use the model to find your unknowns before prompting big work

guidelines: Don't invent an agent-scope taxonomy from scratch: the user's resource-server scopes are the baseline (they're what the subject token carries)
layer additional tool-call-governance scopes on top only for custom MCP servers, or pass the baseline through
data.name: Bootstrap scope definitions from the resource server

guidelines: Deploy one canonical stem
keep every per-user divergence bounded, isolated, immutable, and individually reversible (blast radius = one user context
rollback live, no deploy)
declare what can never be adapted (auth, payments, mandatory fields)
trace every variant back through signal → recommendation → adaptation so bug reports on a program that exists for one user stay debuggable
test correctness across stem + divergences, and separately measure desirability against explicit product goals (retention, churn, support tickets) — a correct change is not necessarily a good one
coordinate updates by merging intent/outcome, not code: users need not run the same commit, they converge on the same goal via their own path
earn autonomy — start where recommendations would be conservative, but build toward a system legible and reliable enough that humans in the loop choose to step back
data.name: Make adaptive software safe with structure, not trust

guidelines: Establish bounded-autonomy guidelines: agents get freedom to generate, inside a centralized scheme of verification and constraints. Never let the generating model validate its own output — use a different methodology (and diversity of tools) to review than to write. Make verification zero-trust (source-agnostic — human or any AI), auditable, explainable, algorithmic and repeatable, so you can prove it ran the same way every time (compliance). Standardize on a single independent multi-layered verification platform across all projects, teams, developers and AI coding tools — silos of per-tool verification create blind spots. Ratchet automation trust: start at find-and-show-and-discuss, enable auto-fix and auto-merge only as confidence accumulates. Equip developers as orchestrators — they design the context frameworks and processes the agents run inside
data.name: Bounded autonomy: free generation, centralized verification

guidelines: Silence is not a terminal state: give runs deadlines and cancellation, add a watchdog so stuck work is visible, give tools timeouts and error results (so a missing result is impossible rather than invisible), and give channels recovery commands that do not queue behind the stuck work they are meant to fix
every external boundary needs an ending — success, failure, timeout, cancel or max attempts — and the receipt must record which one happened so the next step does not have to guess
data.name: Bound the work before the work bounds you

guidelines: (1) Use deterministic logic for facts that can be measured directly
(2) use learning only where contextual action selection adds real value
(3) place safety constraints outside the learned policy so a policy update cannot redefine its own authority
(4) treat escalation and post-action validation as first-class outcomes, not exception paths
(5) evaluate across repeated runs against a simple baseline. Operationally: gather evidence from read-only sources
keep the state compact and the action space small and inspectable (include escalate + log)
write every proposal, execution result, and validation outcome to an audit record
quarantine outputs
represent "safe in principle but unavailable in this environment" explicitly instead of pretending the fix happened
ship via shadow mode (recommend-only) before granting execution authority
data.name: Design self-healing pipeline agents as bounded, auditable deciders

guidelines: Failure modes: an uncurated brain is a garbage dump with great search — retrieval surfaces stale facts with total confidence, and a bad skill file encodes a bad process forever
The primitive is memory plus hygiene: provenance on every fact, contradiction checks when new information collides with old, and a librarian (human + agent) whose actual job is pruning
Dumped-in memory yields a very confident agent that is wrong in ways nobody can trace
data.name: Treat the brain like production infrastructure

guidelines: Compress the page into a ~2k-token markdown representation covering the whole page (vs ~20k raw DOM) and pass it alongside a screenshot
keep end-to-end page-state tracking in the harness
feed explicit diffs each step — new elements, removed elements, cleared blockers, clicks that didn't land — so the agent can diagnose failure instead of blindly re-screenshotting
once the representation is right, downshift to cheaper models for speed and cost
data.name: Give browser agents better eyes, not bigger models

guidelines: Treat context construction as a first-class harness stage with three simultaneous targets — size, flexibility and cacheability — and keep the predictable parts (model instructions) structurally stable so the cache prefix survives
assume the unpredictable parts are user-installed (MCP servers inflating the tool registry, an unbounded skills list) and bound them in code rather than by asking users to install less
mark rarely-used tools deferred so they cost nothing until a tool-search call retrieves them, and supply your own discovery implementation if you can beat the built-in one
cap any growing list as a fraction of the context window rather than a fixed count, and degrade gracefully by shortening descriptions
and remember the reason is quality as much as cost — surplus context raises the odds of self-contradiction, which reads as model confusion
data.name: Budget agent context with mechanism, not discipline

guidelines: Give the agent verbs that fail out loud on a dashboard and keep a human on verbs that fail quietly

put a refilling ceiling on every write (size by namespace: own higher, shared lower) so the agent has full autonomy inside the limit and a loop can only get so bad — and make any bypass flag refuse inside agent sessions and ask the human
watch aggregates, not calls: record every action with the actor's stamp, page when a tripwire crosses, and fix with a sentence of context rather than a code change

size all of it with the undo test — if the agent can put it back and the blast radius is acceptable, log and let it go, otherwise require a second key held by someone else with an audit record (e.g. full canary dial, production promotion only proposed)
keep policy in two places — text for intent, infrastructure for enforcement
and above all stamp identity from a proxy that holds the credentials, never from a header the agent controls, so every quota, approval and tripwire keys on an identity the agent can't change
data.name: Four primitives and one rule for agents with production access

guidelines: Model a constraint graph over space (fit weights + compress agent state history and planning artifacts + reserve render headroom), time (fit agent planning inside the 16 ms / 60 Hz frame or accept jank), and energy (minimize per-loop compute to protect battery until NPUs mature)
use soft-constraining so one axis isn't over-penalized (allow a little extra space, but penalize extra time that disrupts UX)
keep the on-device loop tightly curated for minimum energy
data.name: Budget an on-device game agent across space, time, and energy

guidelines: Define agents as markdown/YAML files that are versioned and reviewed in PRs, dropped into a folder the runtime watches
run them on cron for *when* and on typed events for *because this happened* — each agent declares what it accepts and emits
skip graphs, subscribe to events
keep one append-only, causally linked, queryable event log as the system's memory and add a real queue with attempt counting before you get duplicates
store every prompt part content-addressed so a prompt is a list of hashes and you can trace what the model saw, diff runs, and replay against another model
make typed tool calls and typed events non-negotiable so the kernel makes bad actions impossible
separate kernel (schedule, isolate, journal) from user land (the definitions)
re-evaluate open-source models by replay once observability shows cost
build before you buy while the category is unsettled
and if you sell a framework, eat your own dog food
data.name: Markdown, events, a log, and hashes

guidelines: Ground response logic in validated frameworks (Gottman, EFT): reflect patterns, name dynamics, ask the question under the question, never merely validate
optimize for the user returning to the relationship better, not for sessions
screen every sensitive message in the background for control, fear and risk and switch from coaching to clinician-written protocols when they appear
treat disclosures as privileged and keep them out of engagement analytics and training pipelines
design for immediacy — the intervention before the text is sent
start with the clinician, not the prompt, and encode good as hundreds of TDD-style evals, run tens of thousands of times, with zero tolerance for a failing safety test
and use the product yourself to catch tone drift no eval sees
data.name: Frameworks, screening, privilege, clinician-authored evals

guidelines: Treat intelligence and latency as a flywheel, not a trade-off: optimize losslessly (4-bit math, speculative decoding, KV-cache compression) and spend every gain on more verification
condition ASR on the conversation and the domain (medication list, task, policy), keep prosody, bias on synthetic patient identities, and re-score single-word answers

run a central model with specialist models in parallel, each with a cheap "do I need to speak" check, plus asynchronous verifiers for tool-call parameters and offline verifiers where the workflow allows
benchmark the workflow tasks that matter (labs, IVR) at >99%, and build the benchmark yourself where none exists (empathy)
do the eval math for your volume — hundreds of tests per rare failure — and put licensed clinicians on continuous grading using the human harm scale
make safety an oath the whole company takes
and staff for it with residencies and unlimited tokens
data.name: Own the ear, parallelize the brain, spend latency on intelligence, grade with clinicians

guidelines: Make every primitive hide the infrastructure it handles — the user should see none of the leaky complexity
offer managed sandboxes for on-ramp and self-hosted for serious teams who run their own infrastructure and dev boxes
support multiple harnesses (yours, Claude Code, Codex, custom) but impose platform-native structure so state rehydration and artifacts (PRs, issues, files) behave identically across them
support orchestration of research/implement/validate agents on different harnesses and models, by prompt and by API
expose an API for every primitive — agents, sub-agents, environments, artifacts — so people build on top rather than inside your UI, and expect non-engineers to use it
run your own repository with agents that triage, clarify, spec, implement and gate review before any human is pinged, and let them improve from the examples that accumulate
and design the whole thing as a workshop — event-reactive, observable, self-refining, cost-aware — not a factory
data.name: Absorb complexity, expose primitives, gate with agents

guidelines: Define the target behaviourally — humans write 1–2% of the code, agents run for hours, several in parallel — and measure deployment velocity to production, not commits
prove it on a ladder (pathfinder → structured sprint → a pilot of ordinary teams on existing systems → scale-out) so each confound is answered before the broad rollout
invest in agent context (write down what lived in Slack, onboarding and review
after every agent mistake ask what the skills/steering files were missing
as models improve, prune instructions that now bloat context)
slow down to speed up (better tool error messages, new tools/MCP servers, restructure the code base for agent navigation, consider typed languages, budget ~two months and tell leadership why)
feed, don't babysit (give the task plus how to self-validate
bake the quality bar — compiles, tests, coverage — into the steering file so the agent only returns when it passes)
make intent explicit (BDD/specs
iterate on the document, not on scattered code)
shift testing left (linters, unit/integration/perf/security tests, locally-run deterministic mocks so the loop stays fast on the laptop)
watch for flowmaxxing, parallel-agent cognitive load and review burden on early-career engineers
and speed up decisions — especially reversible ones — because approvals, not code, are now the long pole
data.name: Five habits, one pilot ladder, and an org that accepts the dip

guidelines: Give the judge the agent's harness with read-only permissions so it can inspect final environment state, and explicitly block post-rollout mutations (no redeploys, no writes)
verify state, not the agent's tool-call narration
make the trajectory queryable — persist it, enrich with sub-agents, segment into phases, tag failure points — instead of stuffing it into a context window
keep deterministic verifiers in the loop to produce artifacts and metrics for the judge
never grade open-ended tasks against a single reference answer or sample trajectory
keep rubric density inside what the judge can apply consistently
QA every rubric — gold tests, no-op tests, variance tests, coverage and expert-agreement checks — and escalate that testing as AI takes over rubric authoring and as tasks get longer
data.name: Engineer the judge like an agent

guidelines: Assume the dangerous failures look fine and that omissions and changed decisions, not blatant hallucinations, are the risk
do not trust a pre-specified rubric judge as a safety net — measure how many of its clean passes experts reject
put the system in production and cluster real outputs into a named failure-mode ontology rather than guessing on a whiteboard
have experts leave free-form comments, reasoning and corrections on real outputs in short focused sessions

keep that judgement as indexed examples — past judgments, corrections, references — and assemble a case-specific standard per output by retrieving the nearest judged cases and applicable corrections into the judge's context
make a new correction live on the next call and keep score changes explainable
never freeze the loop, because the standard moves with models, guidelines and institutions
and start today with experts commenting on real outputs — that is the raw material
data.name: Discover from real outputs, capture expert corrections, calibrate per output

guidelines: Route every model call through one gateway with identity, PII redaction, a safety guard under a latency bound, and per-project/user/team attribution for spend guardrails and traces
put an MCP gateway in front of internal APIs (auto-projected) and SaaS tools (hosted, token exchange), then fight the token tax — one omni-MCP, CLI projection, code-mode scripts for heavy uses
pre-provision agent environments with repos snapshotted and indexes built so agents start in seconds, cross-repo
run skills through a managed marketplace with lint, automated review, one-command install, persona auto-install and continuous evals back to authors
build one context graph of how the company runs and plug every skill into it
expose it all through one assistant on every surface
keep autonomous diffs at draft-PR until inner-loop validation (static, visual vs design spec, staging) passes, add self-healing CI and tiered review, and attach the check table to the PR
enroll services in managed maintenance loops throttled to CI capacity and reviewer attention, use landed/not-landed as label data, and turn incident reviews into new skills monthly
and plan for the real bottlenecks — CI, experiments, and deciding what to build
data.name: Six building blocks, then plug the SDLC into them

guidelines: Do not one-shot records with an LLM
reverse your inference workflow — sample the label, derive the reasoning trace, generate backwards
model policies as symbolic decision trees so traces can be sampled deterministically from an appropriate (uniform) distribution rather than the model's prior

generate coarse-to-fine the way the real data is produced (invariants → journey → per-encounter plan → documents), fan out in parallel, and refine with evals for cross-document consistency and a label round-trip
keep everything in text — parse PDFs, don't render them
put domain experts in charge: human-in-the-loop steering at every step and the pipeline itself as skills on an agent harness so experts extend it without engineers
measure fidelity with blind expert review and build datasets just in time per deployment
and apply the same recipe wherever data is ephemeral, sensitive or costly to label
data.name: Reverse the workflow, sample diversity, emulate the process, give experts the keys

guidelines: Start with great human experts and let them determine everything downstream: which tasks the agent performs, how success is measured, what input files and tools it gets
Pair them with someone who has product/business sense for the deployment context (regulation, legal constraints) — domain answers alone don't tell you which tasks matter
Get high-fidelity input data from the real world with real people
synthetic is possible but very hard to do reliably, and obviously synthetic data breeds eval awareness
Make sure the tools work — buggy tools inject noise unless buggy tools are the subject
Align prompts and verifiers in both directions: verify everything the prompt asks, ask nothing the verifier can't see
Design rewards adversarially against a maximally lazy agent
QC everything, and keep a private hold-out set so you don't get contaminated
data.name: Build the benchmark around experts, then verify both directions

guidelines: Ask three qualifying questions first: can you measure the thing, can you apply changes incrementally, can you get feedback on change quality? Then: define the set point (desired end state with respect to one property of the codebase)

build the sensor deterministically wherever possible (ast-grep, ESLint, Packwerk) and out of band from config the agent can disable with an inline comment — an agent plus skill sensor is legitimate where determinism isn't
filter and deterministically sort the violation list
stop the bleeding before migrating — full scan on main, commit the violation baseline to version control, and check every PR for newly added violations (the disturbance dampener)
design the controller explicitly — first violation, or smallest violation to minimise risk, chosen by bash/jq or ast-grep, and never by an agent doing deterministic code's job
enrich the control signal with the data the change is meant to fix (error rates, missing instrumentation, APM gaps) so the actuator improves the code rather than transliterating it
make the actuator an agent plus skill and end the run with a deterministic commit, push, and PR whose body is the agent's final message
data.name: Build the loop as a control loop

guidelines: Treat an agentic media editor as an agentic app builder in a different medium — media+prompt → remote sandbox → agent with tools and skills → rendered artifact — and reuse the coding-agent infrastructure pattern directly
represent the output as code (Remotion / video-as-React) because agents are good at writing code, turning editing into code generation
encode craft as skills (cut rules, font pairs, B-roll generation) and spin sub-processes for music, voiceover, sound and photo animation
run a verification layer that checks the generated composition is clean, well-defined and will render, with a retry loop, since agents make mistakes
consider editing real footage rather than generating as the harder, more differentiated bet (the agent must select best moments and polish messy material, not fill a blank canvas)
and for mass consumer, hide the workflow behind mobile-first directional templates (speak-to-camera, add-B-rolls) so no prompt is needed, with an optional manual editor for tweaks
data.name: Build a media agent like a coding agent

guidelines: Personalize blocks (hero, products, feeds, navigation, CTAs, comparisons), never the whole site, so brand guidelines hold
build a RAG over the site's own content and ground every generation in it
record browsing signals (pages, dwell time, queries) and bucket users into marketer-defined intent groups
let marketers state the strategy in natural language and feed analytics back into it

set a hard 1–2 s page budget and evaluate models *and providers* continuously per site (Promptfoo) on accuracy and latency — expect the answer to differ by site, and prefer a small fast model on fast inference over a large one
pre-generate and pre-fetch "for you" pages from accumulated signals, watching the cost of repeated generations
serve static content and blocks at the edge with the LLM backend behind them
and keep a manual model/temperature switcher for demos and debugging
data.name: Per-user pages: blocks, grounding, and a speed-first model matrix

guidelines: Automate before you hire and add humans at the bottlenecks
launch self-serve first and build the expensive tier from what buyers cannot get
capture rich sign-up data (phone numbers) and answer every inbound automatically
automate outbound research, sequencing and dialing
give buyers no homework — hand-hold, cut pricing options, make paperwork and approvals fast
use pilots sparingly and route around them with references, partial-data evals, demos on their data, opt-out clauses or a one-year POC on a multi-year contract
automate security through a trust portal
price with a base license plus usage and offer caps
hire salespeople when buyers demand a person, choose AI-native sellers, resist up-market early, pay builders on equity and later sellers on simple variable comp
spend on dinners and conferences
treat the first ten customers as design partners
and expect FDEs to be scarce and sticky
data.name: Machine first, self-serve first, no homework, license plus usage, humans at trust

guidelines: Write your own harness rather than adopting an agent framework — in the Claude Code era you get max freedom to tweak anything, and the model writes most of it
use functional tool calling so the whole thing stays provider-agnostic across frontier and open-source models

give the agent three things: full shell (so it writes code, manages its own Python environment, runs things), web search (so it can read arXiv and technical blogs and reach the public state of the art), and a cluster abstraction where it declares hardware needs and submits a job instead of orchestrating hardware

in the research phase, force a to-do list scaffold — prompt it to enumerate everything it must finish before experimenting, so you can re-prompt when it tries to exit early — and make it take per-item markdown notes that later agents query to manage their own context
formulate experimentation as a board so humans can cancel cards, add cards and chat with the strategist
keep an ever-growing leaderboard with a private held-out set and full idea-to-code lineage
design so you rise with the tide of the models rather than having your work consumed by the next one
data.name: Own the harness code; abstract the cluster, not the agent

guidelines: Map your customers' maturity and your product's customizability before hiring
first hires are senior "unicorns" (5+ yrs, technical + customer-facing) — split into specialized roles only at scale
designate SMEs per product area (e.g. long-running cloud agents, SDK) that others pull into projects
hand change management and broad rollouts to SIs/consultancies who know the accounts
say no to wrong-fit use cases — honesty compounds into trust
expect to re-plan profiles and structure every ~6 months
data.name: Build the FDE function to fit your buyer

guidelines: When an LLM "reinvents the wheel every time," give it a domain-intent vocabulary layer rather than a better prompt — let users describe intent in the language they already know (for games: WASD, double-jump, collect-a-coin) and map it to deterministic systems the engine executes

reframe your primitives as tags describing intent (an entity-component-system as tags) that systems query over and that an LLM assistant applies/removes via tool calls, so behavior is declarative and recyclable across projects
manage context with spatial level-of-detail — feed the model full detail for what's near the user's focus and minimal detail for the rest, updating as they move, so context stays small and relevant
and make a large asset library agent-navigable by tagging it with a vision model (screenshot + describe) rather than by hand
data.name: Build tools around domain intent, not primitives

guidelines: Optimize the capture step first, because raw volume is what every later stage feeds on — use voice dictation (~200 wpm, faster than typing for almost everyone) with a hotkey on desktop and phone, and accept scrappy, rambly, unformatted output since structuring is the agent's job
keep everything as markdown in a plain folder so any viewer works and any agent can read it

write enrichment as a skill, not a prompt, and give it two properties that make it schedulable — a per-note enrichment timestamp so reruns only touch unprocessed notes, and a fixed tag vocabulary in a reference folder with explicit instructions to be reluctant to add to it, because agents will otherwise invent a new taxonomy on every pass
have the skill attach sources via web search and generate backlinks by key-term search, so the corpus grows more interconnected with each run

generate wikis over the enriched corpus structured as people, concepts, organizations and sources, which is what turns a pile of notes into something with an index — this works as well for meeting notes and client histories as for personal research

then move the whole loop to a cloud schedule rather than a local one, syncing the folder down (Obsidian headless CLI, or just a git clone), running the skills, and syncing back, so it compounds nightly without your laptop being open
and treat visualizations as disposable — ask an agent for the graph view or the habit chart rather than adopting a tool for it
data.name: Build a knowledge base agents maintain for you

guidelines: Formulate one narrow job per agent (one market, one sector, one parameter) and build as many agents as you need
source the data that differentiates — your own trade theses or failed experiments — and structure it with LLM workflows since nobody will sell it
write the prompt as the expert works, step by step, in logical order
add observability from day one
do not grade with an LLM judge in fields without answer keys
hire the person you sell to and let them curate sources, refine prompts, decompose the problem and judge
climb the ladder in ROI order — error analysis on traces, rubrics as reward (watch for echo chambers), supervised fine-tuning, RLHF (budget to redo it per model release)
treat the loop's outputs as your proprietary dataset

keep the expert deciding (AI-in-the-loop) and ship only when the tool beats the general models on the expert's judgement, because in finance and pharma an agent that does not pay for itself is gone immediately
data.name: Narrow the task, curate what nobody sells, hire the user, climb the feedback ladder

guidelines: Flatten what-the-agent-does and every change-to-the-agent into one immutable typed event log
never edit the graph — only emit events
project state (e.g. the current master prompt) from the log

implement logic as behaviors subscribed to graph changes, including graph-query subscriptions (on object created, if type is claim and it contradicts another claim → trigger contradiction detector) and relation behaviors on edges (research done → unblock write-memo)
do context management as views — a graph query selecting the subset visible to a behavior
encode change control as policies (auto-add research sources; proposed-patch for prompt edits; contradiction checks or human-in-the-loop for facts)
ship capabilities as packs and compose them into agents
data.name: Build the agent around the log, not the LLM

guidelines: Find user tasks that take >1 hour and are (roughly) repeatable — Filed found three in the tax workflow — and build them as long-running background agents
capture skills automatically from product usage to encode the user's way of working (the last 20%)
expose a task list plus per-value traces so every agent-produced value is traceable (this is where trust is built and complaints die)
pause automatically when the agent would make an assumption and let users resolve conflicts by tagging the agent chat-style
present plans for approval before irreversible/dangerous actions
data.name: Build the four pillars of a delegation product

guidelines: Treat deployed-agent traces as the raw material — user prompts and orchestrator-to-sub-agent calls reveal the task distribution before any labels exist
for documents, generate grounded QA pairs, verify answerability with other grounded models, then discard the source
for code, use real PRs, diffs, descriptions and test cases and remove pieces so a known-reachable end state becomes the target

where the back end can't be programmed against (MCP/CLI tools, websites, apps), learn a simulator by iterating between simulation and reality, ground it in production traces, and have agents refine its implementation — then plant answers in it, since you control the state
run it as an online loop (generate, solve, synthesize) gated on pass rate rather than a one-shot dataset build
data.name: Start from the real world, then work backwards

guidelines: Watch the FDE side of your own office before building: the symptom is a 150-page document dump into a chat model and a verbose, wrong answer two minutes later. Ingest what they really work from — meeting notes, documentation, slide decks, email, Slack — and answer the questions they really ask (who owns this process
are these two mentions the same person). Represent the company as a dependency graph as the single source of truth

don't over-think the store (a graph DB and Postgres both work), because the hard part is traversal. Expect frontier models to be too verbose and to have no sense of what a client cares about, so post-train an open-source model for that balance, and train the traversal tools in an RL environment — entity resolution across duplicate names, redundancy-cycle and DAG-violation detection. Embed the assistant where the workflow is actually built so it flags missed edge cases and ownership in place, and let it run beside whatever coding agent the engineer already uses. Automate the routine client minutiae (a mailed request to reroute a report) last, so human time goes to on-site interviews and process design
data.name: Build the assistant your forward deployed engineers actually need

guidelines: Prepare people: tell AI teams to expect change as normal — "change is not a mistake
nobody knew six months ago" — and say it repeatedly, because the rebuild-what-you-just-shipped conversation is a morale and leadership problem before it is a technical one

build to swap: put an abstraction over the agent/model/retrieval approach so the customer-facing behavior stays stable while what's underneath changes, and review every AI choice every six months regardless of satisfaction

define change by evals, not trends: keep eval sets (same input, expected output, graded on cost, speed, quality, capability) and switch only when a new approach beats them — never because of a paper, a demo, or the CEO's link
and choose vendors by change track record: beyond roadmap, ask how they handled the last transitions — those that have reinvented themselves repeatedly are the ones to trust with the next one
data.name: Three moves for infrastructure that expires in months

guidelines: Track the field at 3–4× the old cadence (this is what events are for)
make sure your agent has the capabilities your users need — if something newer/more powerful ships, they will just switch
assume the harness→claw expansion continues (initiative, learning, always-on channels)
even if you top the current hill, plan for the next shakeout wave in the later 2020s
data.name: Position an agent product for the claw era

guidelines: Start from data consistency — one customer data platform with real-time events, referential integrity across CRM, product and third-party entities, attribution and provenance, embeddings over unstructured sales data, pre-computed enrichment and reverse ETL
solve one team's most common workflow first (meeting briefs) and hydrate shared facts once for all consumers
run every trigger as a durable workflow with tool and model calls as resumable activities, config-scoped tool sets and human-in-the-loop pauses
scope retrieval per account with hybrid search rather than stuffing the corpus
let users customize outputs through a skill library
fan out background agents nightly
extend to other teams through skills and integrations
expose the same tools to employees over an MCP and mine their tool-call reasoning to productionize what they build
orchestrate campaigns from intent with channel-owner sign-off, bandit-style explore/exploit and compliance guardrails
and do not spend a year on a perfect architecture — stitch vertical solutions together
data.name: Substrate first, one team at a time, durable agents, federate the tools

guidelines: Treat every harness feature as an encoded assumption about what the model cannot do, write down what that assumption is, and re-test it on each model release — the context-anxiety fix that helped one generation became pure latency and cache overhead on the next, and stale harnesses take weeks or months to migrate precisely when release cycles are shortening

design around a small set of independent primitives so individual components can be swapped without destabilizing the architecture, and aim at the capabilities of the *next* model rather than the current one

decouple the agent loop from the tool-execution environment, which removes container setup from the critical path (measured at ~60% faster time-to-first-token at P50 and >90% at P95), lets sandboxes spin up just in time or be skipped entirely, and isolates faults so a dead sandbox is replaced without killing the run
separate agent, environment and session as distinct resources, and give sessions explicit states including a retry state, so long-running work can always resume where it stopped

persist every event to a durable session log rather than treating the context window as the session — that one decision buys observability, the ability for the model to re-read context it discarded, and the substrate for memory

keep credentials out of the model entirely by decrypting them only at tool-execution time, and offer private execution (self-hosted sandboxes, tunnelled MCP servers) for security-conscious deployments
and define success criteria as a rubric graded by a separate agent so the loop can iterate until the outcome is actually met rather than until the model decides it is finished
data.name: Build harnesses that expect the model to change

guidelines: Delegate by expressing the end state and discussing trade-offs, not by decomposing tasks
be unreasonable — give agents real degrees of freedom (a VM that runs code) and teach users and product teams to ask for more
work multiplayer — delegate in shared channels where ambition is visible, and grow the agent into a proactive teammate with memory
communicate changes as intent artifacts (intention, trade-offs, evidence) rather than raw diffs, verify code with tooling, measure in production, fix forward on cosmetic work
run product bets on a two-week persevere-or-pivot cadence with DRIs who don't manage the pod, and add structure only once something has legs
keep a standing unship list and delete primitives the next generation supplants
pre-measure everything and keep first-class flags and dynamic config
