guidelines: On a hardened target, pass/fail leaves you with almost no information when the model fails

bucketize the exploit chain into rungs and grade each one: trigger the vulnerable line → crash an in-sandbox object → obtain in-sandbox arbitrary read/write (Turing-complete from there) → chain a second vulnerability → obtain out-of-sandbox primitives → arbitrary code execution, using concrete witnesses such as launching a calculator or opening a reverse shell
have a genuine domain expert verify every target is exploitable before you measure
read the ladder position, not the pass rate — and check that the rung you are grading is the one you actually care about (an in-sandbox crash in V8 is expected behaviour, not a hack)
data.name: Get signal out of targets the model cannot beat

guidelines: Report both expert-hours and model-side cost (tokens, steps, tool calls) for every task set
hold model and harness constant before comparing token counts across tasks
treat any cross-vendor hour comparison as invalid unless timing methodology and expert seniority are stated
expect human-hour estimates to degrade as tasks approach top-1% expertise
re-baseline the threshold every model generation (what a generation gains from a bigger context window or better compaction shows up directly as achievable trajectory length)
data.name: Measure horizon on two rulers, and publish the methodology

guidelines: Fine-tuning is expensive and slow to iterate
Instead: episodic memory auto-resolves recurring cases by referencing past similar cases and their decisions (great for recurring false-positive noise)
What still flips escalates to human review

Humans distill the reasoning into semantic-memory rules (e.g., "password spray without successful login → benign; with a final successful login + MFA pass → malicious"), which sharpens the boundary for both the agent and human labelers
data.name: Reach for memory augmentation before retraining

guidelines: Never run analysis scripts over raw object storage — slowest and most expensive path
maintain queryable metadata tables (classic dimensional modeling: star schema / one-big-table) over the raw data
teach the agent to ask "do I have a dataset to answer this in one SQL-ish query?" and, if not, build a layer general enough for the family of questions, not just the one asked
data.name: Answer data questions from metadata layers, not raw binaries

guidelines: Tag source episodes with veracity/origin metadata (e.g. EHR, verified) at ingestion
let all subsequently derived entities and facts inherit the tag
retrieve by walking the graph with a tag filter (e.g. only facts from verified clinical sources) — one tagging action supports fact-veracity evaluation forever after
keep any-parent-vs-all-parents policy in the agent's business rules, not the graph
data.name: Tag provenance once at ingestion, filter at retrieval

guidelines: If the agent must build/run containers, put agent + Docker daemon inside a Firecracker-class microVM with its own kernel
cut the VM off from the host network and route all egress through a vsock to a host process enforcing DNS/hostname/port/CIDR policies
apply separate network policies to the deterministic layer (known egress) vs the agentic layer (ecosystem-dependent egress)
data.name: Sandbox Docker-needing agents in a microVM

guidelines: Ship the agent first — it cannot generate the data you need to improve it until it operates in a real environment — then centralize traces in one project, per-agent or across agents, and point agents at those traces rather than trying to read them yourself, because prompts, tools, skills, hooks, middlewares and agent-to-agent orchestration make behaviour effectively unreadable by inspection

ask trace-level questions a dashboard cannot answer, such as which interactions delighted or upset users, whether quality degrades after the first or second compaction, and how a candidate model would have handled the same task

budget for scale, since cost is input-token price × traces × trace size and long agent traces will not fit in another agent's context — treat a trace as an external object you query into, not material you load
use traces to establish a waterline by starting with a frontier model to prove the task is possible, then reading those traces to work out what guidance a cheaper open model needs to match it
densify your feedback, because a pass/fail number gives an agent almost nothing to act on and traces are the substrate that holds richer signal

and order your work by feedback latency — exhaust harness engineering first at roughly two-minute iterations, fine-tune only to break a demonstrated ceiling and only where the task distribution is narrow, then return to harness engineering
finally, keep humans in the loop for high-trust domains such as legal and medical by preparing trace summaries for review rather than expecting anyone to read it all
data.name: Mine agent traces to improve agents

guidelines: Don't start by hand-writing context: context is hidden in existing business systems and quality compounds across connections

connect Salesforce/HubSpot/warehouse/application layer, reverse-construct how they relate (context is lost at every hop otherwise), then deploy AI on top — Atlan reports "incredible accuracy" for a first-version company brain built this way
data.name: Bootstrap the company brain by reverse-constructing business systems

guidelines: The most valuable intel is never in documentation, and you cannot survey your way to it: your site badge and contractor email address are your data-mining permits, and being a forward deployed engineer in name from a conference room in New York is not the job. Before building anything, establish three things: what the customer is trying to accomplish, what happens after the solution exists, and how they solve it today. Then observe rather than interview — actions speak louder than words. Watch for any task done more than once (per hour, per day, per week), copy-paste between tools, tool or tab switching, phones coming out mid-task, and exasperation phrased as obligation ("well, I have to"). Open with "what's the most annoying part of your morning?" and aim to make their tomorrow different from their today. If the fix is under a day of work, just build it, ship it and close the loop — don't escalate it into a product initiative with PMs attached
data.name: Get badged on site — residents get the truth

guidelines: Look in your own data for a place where you can see a lot of different situations across entities, what those entities did, and how it turned out — that is the one thing off-the-shelf frontier models do not have

then build it into training data: construct states (a detailed point-in-time summary per entity), derive actions from the record itself rather than asking anyone (a campaign was funded, payroll was paid, hiring costs moved), and attach outcomes across multiple horizons (profit, revenue, cash flow, combinations)
assemble state-action-outcome vectors at scale
keep frontier models in the loop for what they are good at — generating candidate actions — and train the grounded model to decide which candidates are right
do not assume the biggest model wins
a mid-size model with the grounding beat the frontier
data.name: Find where your data shows many entities, many actions and verifiable outcomes

guidelines: Map to NIST AI RMF with overhead budgets per level: L1 <5% = bare basics, test-only
L2 5–10% = production minimum (proper logins, encryption, network separation, basic monitoring)
L3 = advanced controls for regulated industries (healthcare, finance)
most teams believe they're L3 but sit at L1–2
run cheap controls everywhere, reserve expensive ones (real-time input detection, heavy isolation) for sensitive/untrusted workloads
data.name: Locate yourself honestly on a maturity model, then climb on purpose

guidelines: Run agents inside tmux on a persistent dev machine (SSH-reachable, portable setup)
expose the session to your phone via a PWA server over a private tunnel — Tailscale default, Cloudflare Tunnel/ngrok work
never expose it on the public internet
use an install skill to bootstrap tmux (or convert an existing tmux config into touch keybindings) rather than hand-configuring
data.name: Get mobile access to agent sessions without changing your workflow

guidelines: Build for multi-model from the start: invest in killing the cache and switching models mid-transcript (doesn't have to be per-thread) — treat the harness as model interoperability
Evaluate cost per capability per second on entire trajectories, not single calls or token price
Switch fast and often
Give labs something back: eval-program partnerships are exchangeable value in negotiations — better than extraordinarily large commits, and no discount is worth the loss of optionality
data.name: The model-agnostic playbook ("this is the slide")

guidelines: State the intent once
select repos by hand or let the dependency graph select them ("find every repo that depends on version X of this library and update it" — the graph knows)
let the harness set up source, dependencies, and a correctly-wired agent per repo at the right SHAs
treat the resulting PRs + CI across repos as a single vector and route failures to whichever side actually needs the patch
capture traces so the session is resumable by anyone
data.name: Treat a multi-repo change as one session

guidelines: Build each task as an environment with multiple *independent* verification channels that fail differently: hidden tests, reference-parity checks, computer-use product checks for UI-bearing tasks, and anti-cheat layers (e.g. strace for forbidden subprocesses like calling GCC in a build-a-compiler task)
run agent trials, inspect failure modes, patch shortcuts and verifiers, and re-run until tasks are both solvable *and* hard to game
treat "zero rollouts rewarded through an exploit" as the bar
publish tasks, logs, and full trajectories so the benchmark is inspectable
data.name: Harden long-horizon evals like an adversary is coming

guidelines: Have the model describe the input and emit structured output before any routing decision
grade that structured output against explicit pass/fail rubric criteria
evaluate the router as a classifier — confusion matrix, precision/recall, n×n when there are more than two branches
generate a per-image prompt from the description plus the router's directives rather than one prompt for everything (a shared prompt collapses catalogue diversity)
score the edit pairwise, input vs output, with yes/no/unsure, and let unsure reject
run the editor against an independent multi-dimensional QA agent for up to K iterations and track pass@K
add a final publish-ready policy-and-quality gate even though it overlaps the in-loop one
prefer a coverage hit over a bad publish
data.name: Gate generated media on named dimensions and iterate against the gate

guidelines: Maintain (or adopt) a table of system invariants — DRAM/NVMe/EBS bandwidth, S3 round-trip latency and cost, per-GB prices across purchase modes — and drill them until they're reflexive (flashcards). Before accepting any benchmark: compute what the operation *should* take (terms × documents × list sizes ÷ DRAM bandwidth

pages visited × ~1ms random SSD read). When benchmark and estimate disagree, treat it as a contradiction to resolve — "one of us is wrong" — and hunt the gap: wrong query plan, accidental distributed fan-out inflating P99, buggy discs, or a hole in your model. Design object-storage systems to P99/P999 (you fire many requests per logical operation, so you *will* hit the tail) and minimize round trips structurally. Batch effects break naive arithmetic (10K MySQL writes/sec on 1ms fsyncs — because fsyncs batch): verify mechanisms, don't stop at the first clean number
data.name: Replace benchmark trust with first-principles accounting

guidelines: Implement agent delegation from all three intake surfaces: issue trackers (Jira/Linear), GitHub issues, and Slack
Let tickets be assigned to agents like sprint members
Keep the flow native so engineers outside the champions program need no new skill
data.name: Wire delegation into where work already arrives

guidelines: Collect the labeling set representatively across the cuts that matter (geography, item type, quality tier, user-generated vs merchant content)
give labelers objective, example-backed guidelines whose purpose is explicitly to remove subjective bias and rater noise
use the *identical* guidelines for the initial golden set and for every later production sample, so offline and online labels stay comparable and mismatch means drift rather than instrument change
align the definition of "better" with product, design, policy and legal before it goes into the eval
hold the golden set as the ship gate for anything the loop retunes
data.name: Make human labels a reusable source of truth

guidelines: Name an owner (system of record) for every fact the agent may use later and make sure it can be replayed
then give that boundary one ordered commit lane — queue or transaction within a session, lock or mutex across sessions
keep parallel reads, independent retrieval, fanned-out sub-agents and concurrent sessions
be conservative at commit time only, never across the whole system
treat "last writer wins" as a bug, not a policy
data.name: Give every mutable state boundary exactly one ordered commit path

guidelines: Pick problems with no ceiling and machine-checkable scoring (compression ratio, proof size, runtime under correctness constraints)
score = task metric + solution complexity so the model can't win by memorizing
use them to elicit novel algorithms rather than benchmark saturation
data.name: Design open-ended evals with a loss function, not a pass/fail

guidelines: Use GitHub Actions / GitLab / CircleCI — they already have code access, secrets, and dispatch plus scheduling primitives

no new cluster. One workflow run equals one iteration (sense, control, actuate, PR), scheduled daily so the team arrives to one small low-risk PR. Label every PR a loop creates so each workflow can identify its own work when several loops run. Add a comment trigger (/iterate) that deterministically loads PR diff, comments, review comments and description into the agent's context alongside the skill. Keep a version-controlled markdown feedback file, load it every run after the controller, and have the /iterate handler update it as well as the code, so steering accumulates in git. Gate the whole workflow on whether any PR with my label is still open, and exit before checkout if so. Scale velocity by having the controller pick 3-5 items with a separate implementation phase per item, or by running the workflow N times for N reviewers
data.name: Operate loops on the CI you already have

guidelines: Track token usage and cost per team and individual across all vendors (build cross-vendor dashboards if you mix tools) but treat it as a smoke detector — adoption gaps and bursts — never a leaderboard
don't cut cost before you can measure value
measure value as trusted throughput — complexity-weighted merged PRs (LLM t-shirt scoring) that pass objective checks, human review and customer contact

expect the bottleneck to move to review and CI: put AI review first for style and coverage so humans spend judgment on architecture and security, invest in flaky-test removal and CI speed, and watch ready-to-merged time vs CI duration and PR retry counts
discourage giant PRs that dodge slow CI
set guards (budgets, quotas, anomaly alerts), review metrics regularly in context, and close a learning loop with individuals
teach token hygiene — cap loop steps, put the fixed system prompt first for prefix caching, prune or auto-compact context
buy the non-differentiating (IDE, CI) and build the shared prompt playbook
and sit with resistant engineers to find the high-impact work that still grows them
data.name: Measure value before cutting cost; fix review and CI

guidelines: Provide tool access plus role-specific immersive training (Automattic: two-week course per employee, lectures + hands-on)
Invest in security, processes, and dev-env documentation that non-engineers can follow
Expose institutional knowledge to AI tools (internal MCP over documentation)
Run a bounded experiment window with roadmap paused (30 days, two-person teams, full autonomy, "ship something real", staged thirds of the company)
Find enablers and champions
Grant agency so people break out of habitual processes — start at team level if you can't do it company-wide
data.name: Roll out org-wide AI building in a large company

guidelines: Instrument scoring inside the execution layer where inputs, outputs, and the full trace already flow
defer scoring as a task after execution completes
attach real-world outcome events to the session (triage → did the engineering team act? research agent → was the report saved?) instead of thumbs-up/down

close the loop with a scheduled reviewer function that reads execution logs (what ran, what sub-agents fanned out, what workflows were called), evaluates system performance, and adjusts prompts/metrics or reports what to improve
data.name: Score agents on outcomes attached to sessions

guidelines: Score memories by semantic similarity × historical utility (did this memory help or hurt past executions)

submit failures as explicit feedback so trajectories change (demo: "find me a gaming mouse" returned nothing → failure submitted → next run reformulated to wireless mouse and succeeded, with a visibly changed tool-call trajectory)
expect a cold-start phase of pure semantic retrieval until reviews accumulate
guard against utility drift and noisy review labels
tune the lambda credit/re-ranking hyperparameter
data.name: Make retrieval learn from outcomes

guidelines: On agent completion, run an executor the agent doesn't control: lint agent code (send back on failure — fail early), detect cross-edit conflicts, run the code, validate output artifacts, then emit a structured review artifact — e.g. an emissions report: which edit functions ran, 749 edit actions across 50 graphs, −45.6% overall emissions, drill-down per graph and node — so users and reviewers never read the underlying code
false completion claims surface automatically and loop back to the agent
data.name: Own final execution and make review code-free

guidelines: Zero CVEs today ≠ safe: unmaintained packages patch slowly when the next CVE lands
Prefer active maintenance + usage
Automate via health-check tool in a skill/hook
data.name: Choose dependencies on health, not just CVE absence

guidelines: Build A/B pairs, not 1–10 labels
manufacture the bad half (corrupt good footage, generate slop) but audit what the pairs actually teach — coherence shortcuts are the default failure
keep encoding identical on both sides of every pair
annotate both sides with the identical method
pair real footage against AI footage to break the gloss shortcut, while watching for the opposite failure of the model degenerating into an AI detector
distill the committee (frame metrics + frontier judges + human labels) into a small VLM once you have the labels
pick the base model you already know how to post-train
data.name: Train a media judge on comparisons, not scores

guidelines: Keep dangerous credentials (git write, PR creation, CI trigger, registry write) in a deterministic orchestrator
agent output = file edits only
vet the diff for nonsense (empty files, stray binaries) before the deterministic layer commits
prompt-steer the agent away from known-untrusted context (vendor/ dirs, CI logs)
maintain an injection-eval honeypot repo (deprecated functions + migration guides that try to recruit the agent) and run the agent against it
data.name: Partition agent blast radius by architecture

guidelines: (1) Every claim comes with a receipt — each sentence linked straight to its source paragraph with the source's trust level attached, not a citation tab at the end
(2) facts and guesses stay visibly separate — at a glance on the page, what is proven versus what is someone's best estimate, labelled in a way that survives copy-paste into someone else's slides
(3) numbers agree with each other automatically — the system refuses to ship a document whose figures don't match, with no human checking at 2 a.m.
(4) contradictions get surfaced, never smoothed over — when sources disagree the system raises its hand instead of picking the more fluent answer
(5) a real human approval gate, logged — who reviewed what, what changed, when they signed
that log is the audit trail
then test it with the 30-second challenge: point at any sentence and demand its source — one click, or seven tabs
data.name: The five things a buyer demands before a system goes near a live deal

guidelines: Keep it as markdown in one central Git repo — not a vector store — so it is both human- and agent-readable and authorable, and keep it central: team- or product-scoped catalogs lose the whole benefit, which is that a pattern confirmed by one service's profiling run is free for every other service's agent. Give each entry query hints and symbols, the services where it was confirmed, a confidence level that rises with each confirmation (higher confidence means more willingness to open a code review), and both the anti-pattern and its good-pattern counterpart. Starting empty is fine

bootstrapping is faster — Jeff Dean's C++ optimization notes, PyTorch's torchfix catalog, and your own existing performance playbooks. Generalize entries across languages and frameworks where the underlying problem is universal (quadratic loops, loop invariants, per-iteration allocation, batchable contention). Let humans author entries too, especially while building new frameworks and platform components, when they have the most context. Structure and index it hierarchically so an agent navigates to the relevant entry instead of loading the catalog into its context window — this is what makes it usable at authoring time rather than only at review time
data.name: Build the anti-pattern catalog as fleet-wide agent memory

guidelines: Have the agent read the rendered interface (layout/state/what changed), not scraped code
complete the loop by checking its own output instead of firing actions and moving on
capture user input by pointing/annotating on-screen elements (an exact, low-loss instruction) rather than long text
write design rules in a design.md and have the agent turn them into a visual on-brand check plus an automated user-flow walkthrough, emitting a pass/fail report a human reviews
extend "perception" beyond the screen — e.g. ambient meeting audio via a wearable → transcript → applied changes
data.name: Give agents perception plus self-verification for unverifiable work

guidelines: Partially apply the risky parameter (e.g. lock `read`/`write` to one directory) before passing the function as a tool: the LLM never sees the locked argument in the schema, so the agent physically cannot escape the boundary — autonomy without approval fatigue, capability without blast radius
data.name: Lock dangerous tool arguments with partial function application

guidelines: Two selection criteria, both stated as decisive
Your own domain expertise determines the achievable data quality — data is boutique now, and you cannot manufacture realism in a field you have not worked in

The clarity of the users' problem statement determines whether a whole company can be simulated at all: infrastructure qualifies because the users' wants are unambiguous and stable (a Modal user wants GPU sandboxes with low latency and low cost that do not fail halfway through a training run), whereas a pre-product-market-fit startup does not, because nobody in it yet knows what correct looks like
Then go deep on one vertical and expect the lessons — not the environments — to transfer horizontally
data.name: Choose the domain by expertise and by clarity of the problem statement

guidelines: Keep all three tiers and route by problem shape: deterministic checks where the output is structurally checkable
LLM-as-judge with a fixed rubric and fixed scores where the flow is stable and the failure set is known in advance

agent-as-judge — a long-running agent reading the trace stream — where each interaction produces a different trajectory (dynamically generated UIs, sub-agents, long-horizon loops) and the failure modes are not enumerable ahead of time
Run evals on live production traces, not only offline: that is what shows what's working, catches the failures, and produces the data that fuels continual-learning loops

Expect the discovered failures to be ones you would not have written a rubric for (same tool called repeatedly, inefficient trajectory, no done-detection), and wire the discovery straight through to a fix
data.name: Choose the eval tier by how variable the trajectory is

guidelines: At equal disk size, prefer the big model quantized (intelligence-per-byte wins)
but check decode speed against your GPU — a big quant at 5–10 tok/s may lose to a small native model at 200 tok/s for interactive use
split the difference with routing (big model plans, small model executes)
respect runtime defaults that keep tiny models at higher precision (very small models quantize badly)
and remember lab-released small natives (Nemotron Nano, Gemma small tiers) exist precisely for the cases where the quantized giant is impractical
data.name: Big-quantized vs small-native is a throughput decision

guidelines: Never bare fork/exec (kernel exposure + noisy neighbor)
containers (namespaces/cgroups + seccomp) still share the host kernel and seccomp allowlists break agent products
gVisor leaves a two-step chain to the host
use a Rust-based micro VM with jailed virtio devices
accept the trade-offs — VM-exit overhead, reactive balloon-driver memory reclaim, GPU passthrough (VFIO) is single-tenant
data.name: Skip the seven stages: micro VMs from day one

guidelines: Keep human code review
small stuff still goes straight to the agent. For the rest run a four-stage pre-alignment: (1) product review — problem, desired behavior, mockups
(2) system architecture — component contracts, data models, constraints
(3) program design — types, method signatures, layout, call graphs (underemphasized; don't assume the model "can cook" from architecture alone)
(4) vertical slices — implementation order, multi-repo coordination, checks along the way. Diagnosis: you don't have too many PRs, you have too many bad PRs — a well-aligned PR is a joy to review
even 20% rework is an emotional and intellectual burden on both sides
data.name: Turn the lights back on: plan up front, read every line

guidelines: Run a check that reads the actual output after generation, with power to block shipping
Soft-flag via regex honesty inspector (did it answer the question? did it hedge?) — regexes are fast, cheap, deterministic
Choosing determinism over a small classifier's coverage is a real trade-off to make consciously
Hard-reject any number, date, or fact not present in an allow-list of known-true values
Build the veto as one shared service every surface passes through by default (per-surface wiring is a checklist waiting to be forgotten)
Centralize condition/mode resolution in one resolver rather than per-surface knowledge
data.name: Gate output with a deterministic post-generation veto

guidelines: When compliance is enforced by an ever-growing rule list in the prompt and latency is the casualty: collect the product's own logs, curate prompt/response pairs from them, tag the spans that carry the required form so the model learns structure rather than memorizing skewed values (imbalanced numerics are where post-fine-tune hallucination comes from), fine-tune, and measure compliance, latency and throughput together
Expect the ownership benefit to be part of the business case — the enterprise stops re-engineering prompts under each frontier release and stops paying frontier prices
data.name: Move rules out of the prompt and into the weights

guidelines: Run the loop brainstorm → plan → work → review → polish → compound → repeat
keep your brain on at the ends — decide the problem yourself at the start (block time, don't multitask) and raise the bar at the end
whenever you repeat yourself, extract it into repository solution documents (reasoning, decisions, postmortems, taste rules) so it never happens again
spend 50% of time teaching the system what it got wrong
work the middle manually until an overnight or three-hour run is always good, then let it rip in parallel
document the thinking, not the code
use or build the tooling — ideation against OKRs, doc review, brainstorm, an overnight loop with before/after evidence, polish, compound
and hold the standard that the next feature should be easier because you shipped this one
data.name: Extract, never repeat; brain at the ends; make the middle boring

guidelines: Score two axes: how attributable the outcome is to your product, and how much agency/autonomy your product has to achieve it. Weak attribution means seat-based (the historical default). High autonomy with weak attribution means usage-based (the foundation-model API shape). High on both — a resolved support inquiry, a completed sale — means outcome-based, which is where agentic products belong and where the market is heading. Two consequences to plan for: outcome pricing is not always available, so be honest about which quadrant you are in
and once you price the outcome you must staff a function accountable for guaranteeing it, which is the structural reason vendors are building FDE orgs at all
data.name: Place the product on the attribution x autonomy grid before choosing a pricing model

guidelines: Six steps: (1) pick a figure with both a primary record and a saturating cultural composite (the Miranda condition)
(2) identify 3–4 documented moments where the figure's reasoning demonstrably differs
(3) with a domain expert, write diagnostic questions on those fault lines (test argument architecture, not recall)
(4) run three seeding conditions — primary sources, modern biography, bare model
(5) score blind on the three-axis rubric
(6) report, confirm or refute, and publish corpus + questions + rubric + predictions before data exists
data.name: Replicate the pre-registered compositing experiment

guidelines: Decide per use case which of availability, latency, guardrails and cost you protect in a degradation, and expose those levers

replace retries and circuit breakers with per-request fallback across providers behind a normalization layer (tool schemas, token limits, stop reasons), cool down failing primaries, choose instance-local vs fleet-wide failure counts deliberately, and provision the fallback provider with *more* headroom
accept that streaming forfeits fallback mid-stream
track P99 per model per route, set timeouts per model class per route, fix reasoning levels, make router-model requests as deterministic as possible, and hedge the tail at P90

treat guardrails as unreliable dependencies — fail-open or fail-closed by the worst case you can live with, give them time budgets and fallbacks, and place them pre-hook, parallel (structured outputs, no streaming) or post-hook (audit)
segregate keys and limits per route, support load shedding and bounded queues, prioritize traffic
and prefer centralized governance over decentralized traffic to a single company-wide gateway deployment
data.name: Fallback, not retry; per-route everything; governance without a chokepoint

guidelines: Keep bounded contexts isolated and asynchronous — don't let agents read across them
append commands as immutable events rather than mutating state
drive propagation with CDC/change feed where the store supports it and with the message broker where other teams don't practise event sourcing
put a worker process between the stream and the view to massage and denormalize (counts, averages, recent activity, trust scores, KYC status, account age)
land the result in one materialized "semantic" view and expose it to agents only through tools
keep separate read models for separate purposes (timeline, customer, risk) instead of one general store
never serve agent reads from the event store itself
data.name: Project your event stream into an agent-facing semantic layer

guidelines: Keep prompts short and objective-level (roughly half of SWE-bench Pro's 4,500-character average) so the agent has to explore and derive its own to-do list — that is the realistic shape of a task handed to a junior engineer or an agent — and check that terse prompts still yield long-horizon work by measuring solution size (5x LOC, ~7 files touched, 2x output tokens) rather than prompt size. Say nothing about whether to write tests: any instruction there overwrites the self-verification behaviour you were trying to measure. Run scoring rollouts through one deliberately minimal agent-agnostic harness, and validate that choice with control runs on each model's native harness
data.name: Control the prompt and the harness, or you aren't measuring the model

guidelines: Remove examples — frontier models (Opus 4.8/Fable-class) are more creative without them
prefer context over "do not X" (hard constraints collide confusingly with later user/skill instructions)
audit every instruction for the 10% of cases where it's wrong and soften until it's 100% accurate ("always verify" → when/why verification helps), because the model receives it 100% of the time
maintain per-model system prompts — weaker models still need the verbose version
data.name: Prompt frontier models with context, not constraints

guidelines: Have property-based tests created from the requirements + design documents and actually executed (fast-check in TS runs each property dozens-to-hundreds of times with randomized values) so task implementations are machine-checked against the spec, e.g. "for any movie data set the extracted genre list must contain exactly a sorted set of unique genres" (paraphrase of demo)
data.name: Generate and run property-based tests against the spec

guidelines: Keys live and persist only on the user device — the backend never stores them
encryption has no opt-out and no bypass path
client releases keys only after an attestation pipeline verifies node integrity AND that the workload is in a public transparency log (Sigstore)
replicate keys only to attested confidential-compute nodes, scope-limited per node
run inference inside the perimeter (unencrypted data never leaves)
force in-memory key expiry sized to the usefulness horizon (Bee: 7 days — 24h loses offline users)
split release power: a separate team's signing keys are hardcoded into clients and backends so your own team can't ship unnoticed
keep the TCB tiny (~20k LOC, memory-safe) and reuse vetted crypto — "don't invent your own" (Telegram lesson)
use a private CA to embed attestation proofs in certs (public CT logs would leak the fleet)
data.name: Build an agent backend you provably can't read

guidelines: Fill out the agent-facts form (host39.org for individuals/small businesses) → get an agent card → publish to the Nanda index
enterprises: run your own catalog and register your gateway from your own domain
existing websites: attach agents to domains via DNS records
ensure the agent stays reachable — self-host for control or use cloud/agent-hosting (sleep/wake platforms cut idle cost)
data.name: Put your own agent on the open agentic web

guidelines: Heuristic: if agent reliability is "a coin flip," stop prompting and pull the control flow out. Model the workflow as a state machine
hand the model one single-step contract per turn
validate its output in the harness
let the harness (not the model) decide the next state. Generalizes beyond voice — coding agents, ops runbooks, onboarding flows
data.name: Take control flow out of the model

guidelines: Put SFT-style question/answer and chat data — and agentic traces, which fit because many models now pre-train at long context anyway — into the pre-training mix, so the model learns conversation and task shapes from the start instead of meeting them as a distribution shock later

For MoE models this is also a stability measure: without it, the pre-/post-training distribution gap causes severe expert imbalance, and the available fix (raising the load-balancing coefficient during SFT, as MAI reported) means changing the balance far into training, which you should not want to do
Treat mid-training — post-training/RL distribution plus longer context — as the designed bridge, and consider pulling those datasets back further still
data.name: Move post-training-shaped data backwards, don't patch at the boundary

guidelines: Wrap the robot's preset functions and trained policies as tools (Strands' robot package covers many robots) and let an agent choose among them from natural language
run separate concurrent agents for thinking, communicating (chat, web, Telegram) and voice, and disable the ones that would collide on stage
keep the split — the agent decides what, the policy decides how — across agent, policy-provider, backend and hardware layers
train policies and VLAs in the cloud and call inference on the edge for latency, letting the agent pick
give the system prompt the rules and tool descriptions plus safety guardrails
use the running robot to generate training episodes from manual runs and its own reasoning
and plan for the agent layer to shrink as robot foundation models grow
data.name: Expose policies as tools, split what from how, train in the cloud, act on the edge

guidelines: Surround the agent loop with checks: type-validate tool parameters with Pydantic at the boundary
run tool results through an ontology-backed reasoner before accepting them into records
keep agents side-effect-free until validation passes — no database writes pre-check
on an unreasonable result, loop back to the LLM or bring a human into the loop
remember the LLM can't execute anything — it only proposes tool calls, so the checkpoints are yours to place
data.name: "Pydantic at the door, ontology at the ledger"

guidelines: Need, not want: only build FDE if you must GTM a technically complicated product to a non-technical buyer — otherwise run DevRel (technical buyer) or sales-led SaaS (simple product). Second gate: have a platform, or commit to building one

FDEs must assemble from shared primitives, never write from scratch. Set primitive granularity by customer breadth — some domains tolerate apps that ship 60% built with 40% customization, others need extremely granular configuration and tooling (AWS is the reference point). Keep anything bespoke to a single customer with that customer
generalize anything generalizable over time. Expect thin primitives at the start — that is fine, FDE also scouts which products to build next
data.name: Qualify (and platform-back) an FDE function before you build one

guidelines: Uniform/random compression at 86% doesn't make a model 86% dumber, it makes it 100% dumber — exploit structure instead. First and last layers are critical, middle layers compressible
keep linear-attention projections and QKV layers high-precision (quantizing linear attention passes benchmarks then breaks long context)
vision/audio layers stay 8/16-bit
sparse MoE layers take aggressive quantization
choose layers via calibration data + gradient-based sensitivity analysis (LP/knapsack solvers automate it)
treat selection as combinatorial (layer pairs/triples, per-tensor decisions), and hunt super-weights — one wrongly quantized number can cost 20% of capability. PTQ works out of the box ≥~20–30B dense
below that use QAD — with the *right* data, since wrong-data QAD usually breaks the model
data.name: Leverage the architecture; never quantize uniformly

guidelines: Any input whose size scales with job duration (time series, logs) must not touch the parent context
Convert to bounded artifacts (annotated image collages) and analyze in a dedicated sub-agent that returns only a findings summary
Give each role agent its own prompt + tool subset — scope expansion then becomes "add a prompt" (how Medic gained Spark-SQL optimization)
data.name: Quarantine token-heavy analysis in sub-agents

guidelines: Decide honestly whether you are competing on the ceiling or the floor, because the answer determines your whole evaluation strategy — and note that user trust and most visible AI harm are governed by the worst thing your agent can do (recommending a competitor, deleting data, emailing a customer something it should not have) rather than the most impressive

keep evals as tests in code run locally, not curated datasets in a playground, since the prompt is now your entire harness and any dataset built against one model or harness breaks when you switch — and be wary of investing months in eval infrastructure you will not actually let delay a model upgrade

for production triage, remember that clusters are not issues: they cannot be tracked reliably over time, their boundaries are not yours to control, and they merge unrelated root causes — instead make every issue carry when it started and what percentage of users it affects, since the first turns a report into an investigation and the second is what makes it worth doing
scale analysis with code mode over traces, writing classifiers as code and running them in a sandbox at production volume rather than feeding traces to a model

keep detection deterministic and investigation agentic, because agents are bad at finding anomalies and good at explaining ones you hand them — pull out what you can with simple signals like keyword frequency first

and size your approach to your user count, since experiments and free-tier A/B tests are extremely valuable at millions of messages a day and actively wrong at five users, where a single internal enterprise app may still be critical to get right
data.name: Raise the floor before chasing the ceiling

guidelines: Treat popularity as zero evidence of validity — the loudest benchmarks are selected for incumbency and marketing, not for measuring value
Check whether the model card discloses contamination
assume it doesn't, because the industry has no such habit
Ask whether the verifier can actually separate a strong model from a weak one — if two very different models land on the same score, the task is noise
Watch for evals run under undisclosed conditions and for silent multi-candidate testing
Read "saturated at 80%" as possibly meaning "the last 20% is broken"
And remember what the benchmark is a proxy for: if the score is climbing while human eval is flat or falling, the score is the thing being optimized
data.name: Read benchmarks as a consumer who assumes misalignment

guidelines: Never accept "forward deployed engineer" as a specification — decide which vintage the work actually is: platform stability/DevOps (2008), data integration and data modelling into your ontology (2012), custom solutioning on top of integrated data (2016), customer enablement so thousands of their engineers do the work (2020), or end-to-end agent building against a contracted outcome (2024+). Ask the candidate which vintage they are and check it against the vintage you need

expect the eras to be additive rather than exclusive, so a real posting stacks skills instead of trading them. Treat the composite mega-posting (staff engineer + direct sales + solution architect + teaching) as a symptom of skipping this step
data.name: Hire and scope against a vintage, not a title

guidelines: Don't prompt an LLM for "50 test queries": sample real production conversations, mutate criteria to cover golden paths and edge cases
fine-tune the user LLM on real user verbatims (terse, impatient, frustrated)
define user personas (bypasser, refund seeker, AI skeptic) and world state (e.g. long-tenured luxury driver)
accept that eval scores drop — that's the realism working
data.name: Make the user simulator as difficult as production

guidelines: (1) Use a Haiku-class fast model on an inference platform that prioritizes latency (judge by P95, not size/price), with deliberately short context

hand heavier work to a larger model asynchronously and re-interleave its results into the real-time stream. (2) Send inference eagerly every 1–2 seconds while the user is still speaking instead of waiting for a second of silence — turn-end waiting alone blows a 1s budget. (3) Run a stable caching regimen: keep the first ~90% of the context identical across requests to exploit prefix caching (up to ~90% cheaper/faster), and minimize output tokens. Human limits to design against: ~100ms feels instant, ~1s is the train-of-thought limit, ~200ms is the conversational-voice floor
data.name: Hit the real-time envelope for voice-in/visuals-out agents

guidelines: Give every node a keypair for identity + signing
sign every interaction step into one chain (descriptor → offer → quote → deal → invoice → receipt) so tampering with any link breaks it
use a marketplace node only for service description/indexing, then let requester and provider communicate peer-direct (no middleman) in one interaction: request, sign, execute, receipt
split payments into a base payment (protects providers from request flooding) and a success fee (protects requesters from malicious providers)
require a shared interface, not a shared software stack
data.name: Design agent-to-agent transactions as tamper-evident receipt chains

guidelines: Network capture misses half the agent (local retrieval, in-process tools, memory) and shreds under streaming/async
wrap each node (tool / LLM / retrieval) and record what enters and leaves it — the meaning of each step, not the packets
know and log your session variables (LLM version, build ID, RAG chunks, sampling params)
capture the full envelope, not just the prompt
data.name: Record agent runs at node boundaries, not the network layer

guidelines: Record mode: agent calls real downstream systems, tool responses captured as fixtures and checked in as code
Playback mode: agent runs against fixtures and produces the report
Grade reports with authored offline evals (e.g. penalize >3 suggested fixes to control verbosity)
Tune prompts against scores
Add OTel traces (→ LangFuse) and read the run as a waterfall to localize quality drops
data.name: Build a record/playback eval harness for production agents

guidelines: Build paired eval sets: routine tasks a working practitioner would actually ask, and red-team tasks that look innocuous but carry harmful structure (a benign-labelled sequence that is really a toxin)
score both rates

Treat over-refusal on routine domain work as an eval failure to be fixed with the same seriousness as an under-refusal on the adversarial set — in the measured case the routine set was refused far more often than the adversarial one
data.name: Test refusals in both directions

guidelines: Hand it reference code that represents what you want — even from a different system or language — or an HTML mock-up for a React component, with "read this, understand it, then start"
a working artifact encodes the unknown-knowns a prose spec misses
data.name: Give Claude another map instead of writing a spec

guidelines: Model chooses UI from a fixed component menu — it never invents components
maintain a version→capability repository and surface a component to the model only for client versions that support it (new flight card in 2.0 → only from 2.0 onwards)
make the model emit typed blocks — conversation blocks for text, UI blocks for render intent
encode layout rules in the contract (1–3 flights → swipeable carousel, 4+ → vertical list)
context engineering is what makes the model pick correctly as surfaces multiply
data.name: Give the model a typed, versioned rendering contract

guidelines: Pre-PMF: rent (Airbnb the city before buying the house). Post-PMF or a budgeted enterprise project: build owned infrastructure. Check the three enterprise walls beyond cost — control (rate limits), audit (third-party dependency), reproducibility (model internals access). Even while renting, optimize the layer you control: input-token compression, context management, taming wasteful agent-loop calls. Expect memory to be the bottleneck when moving to local hardware (DGX-class)
data.name: Decide when to stop renting inference

guidelines: Pick a sandboxable scripting language models know cold (JS here
Python would work equally well)
keep heavy domain logic in the right implementation language behind it (C# here)
expose new capabilities as runtime methods documented by a TypeScript type-definitions file in the prompt — no tool-schema churn
keep state persistent across calls so the agent interleaves reasoning between steps
avoid rigid multi-agent phase splits — Witan's three-agent define/plan/execute/verify pipeline was a dead end because discovery ran once up front and context didn't flow between agents
data.name: Consolidate agent tools into a persistent REPL

guidelines: Accept that line-by-line review is already gone (a large share of changes merge unreviewed) and that reviewing has become the bottleneck — but do not conclude "no review," because review's real function is alignment (knowledge sharing, architecture, mentorship) and that must survive
separate the two halves — automate semantic accuracy, keep humans on alignment

capture intent from the agent session, not the code, since the real decisions are made in the prompts and get thrown away at PR time, and since an agent that wrote the code cannot be trusted to write the test plan that catches its own issues

turn captured session responses into acceptance criteria, and build an AI slop registry by mining your recurring review comments so each becomes an automatic guardrail that compounds with every merge (expect a J-curve before payoff)
compile criteria plus registry into a test plan and verify it against a live preview end-to-end, collecting evidence (screenshots, DB snapshots) — because working matters more than looking right
make that verification output the review surface, so reviewers examine intent and evidence rather than the diff and can discuss architecture one level up
keep it deterministic where possible and LLM where necessary, and write the test plan in English so PMs and designers can participate
data.name: Replace line-by-line review with intent-and-evidence verification

guidelines: Replay the recorded trace with every node stubbed except the one you changed (fix at the tool/guardrail layer — you cannot control the LLM)
assert on the changed node's output
keep the trace as a permanent regression test in CI
and keep generation-time variation alive — don't pin temperature to zero, "that is what brings the agency into your agent" (paraphrase)
data.name: Run the loop: annotate → record → visualize → understand → fix → replay → verify

guidelines: Add context files (agents.md / claude.md)
Rules files as guardrails
Repeatable workflows (slash commands, later agent skills)
An AI code reviewer with instructions on what matters
AI attribution on PRs
For monorepos, set shared context/rules at the root and layer service-level overlays (inheritance)
Don't force one-size-fits-all — web ≠ mobile; let similar-shaped teams converge on tools
data.name: Make repos AI-ready before demanding delegation

guidelines: (1) Prove it's possible at all with the largest capable model

(2) define success measures up front — output validity (e.g. JSON parses), reference/structural validity, factual consistency (LLM- or human-judged), length compliance, P50/P95 latency budgets (here P95 ≤3.5 s against the 4 s believability limit) — and export a golden dataset of curated, preferably human-labeled input→output pairs as ground truth
(3) test candidates from small to large against the criteria (here: Qwen 2.5 1.5B, Qwen 3 1.7B, Llama 3.2 3B, Gemma 4 E2B vs a Claude Sonnet ceiling — the fastest model, Qwen 2.5, lost on accuracy)
(4) select the smallest model with acceptable responses
Framework built with Google, published on web.dev
data.name: Right-size the model in four steps ("prototype big, deploy small")

guidelines: RL only works if P(good answer) > 0: warm up with SFT/priming so the format is reachable
expect long zero-reward stretches ("patience is all you need... luck is all you need")
outcome-only rewards credit broken reasoning, so move toward process supervision — but remember LLM-judged process supervision inherits the self-verification problem
watch for environment destruction (rm -rf class outputs), not just reward hacking
data.name: Make RL able to find the reward at all

guidelines: (1) Cheapest: wrap an RLM as a CLI tool the agent can call when a task exceeds context (e.g., sifting a 100M-token corpus). (2) On Claude Code: use dynamic workflows — study the six patterns in "A Harness for Every Task," and know the difference between a hard-coded map-reduce workflow and a true RLM workflow where the model picks the decomposition. (3) Harness-agnostic: write a .prose.md program — declare the sub-agent decomposition, wire skills/CLI tools in as explicit dependencies so each sub-agent is provably equipped, verify sub-agent output in the parent session. Set recursion depth deliberately — "recurse responsibly"
data.name: Three routes to make a coding agent recursive

guidelines: Treat making engineers work well with agents as an organizational responsibility, since the highest-leverage changes are to shared codebase organization and no individual can make them — and because uneven adoption is self-entrenching, with fast adopters' PR volume landing as review burden on slower colleagues who then have less time and more reason to distrust the tools

diagnose the setup rather than the model when things go wrong — babysitting, "the model is dumb today" (the model did not change), silently burning 500k–1M tokens and hitting auto-compact on simple tasks, long sessions needing constant intervention, and a steady slop output are all setup symptoms

do progressive disclosure properly and measure it — keep the agent instruction file a thin index that points to files rather than one loaded document, cap skill files around 100 lines since a skill is really a folder, put runbook documentation in code comments so a grepping agent finds it in place, then watch the first prompt's context cost and treat 40–50K where 20–25K is baseline as a failure
harvest your best ICs' practices and ship them as the shared setup, accepting that engineers dislike being told their personal setup is imperfect

invest in one high-value end-to-end skill rather than broad mandates, and expect a long-running one (code-done to PR-ready, including CI failure loops) to convert skeptics precisely because it proves the agent can be left alone
close the loop with CI, agentic reviews and a nightly code-gardener, because slop is inevitable and needs a detection-and-repair path
budget a standing percentage of IC time for setup work that produces no PRs
give experiments and prototypes an explicit opt-out from your production standards rather than letting them drag the bar down
and treat winning over skeptics as the real measure — you know they are bought in when they edit the shared setup themselves
data.name: Roll agents out as a leadership programme, not an IC exercise

guidelines: Instead of always stuffing the latest messages: after n messages keep a running summary plus only the ~n−5/n−10 most recent messages
Answer "remember that thing we talked about?" by doing recall over the rolling summary rather than retaining full history — cheaper than token-limit overload on long threads, works with legacy models
data.name: Handle long conversations with a rolling summary plus recall

guidelines: Read every line of authentication, money movement, permissions, and irreversible-data changes — inspect the critical path yourself
ask your agents ("clankers") to map which files/primitives in a large repo are critical
decompose long diffs into atomic reviewable PRs (agents are good at decomposing — ask them)
keep classical verification — traces, evals, shadow mode
separate the builder from the verifier: never let the agent that wrote the code also write the tests and grade the output (writing your own exam and scoring it)
when a human catches a mistake in review, encode it once — documentation, linter rule, reviewer memory — so the *system* catches that bug class forever
engineer rails, observability, and rollback rather than re-spending attention per change
data.name: Route every change to the proof it needs (the "Monday artifact" routing table)

guidelines: Don't route on task type: agentic complexity mutates mid-session, so think in subtasks/phases and re-decide as the session evolves. Keep frontier intelligence present even when it isn't working — a watcher that detects the delegate going down a rabbit hole
piggyback those checks on cache refreshes you were paying for anyway ("a free frontier call"). Prefer one persistent sidekick over sub-agent fan-out (running context stays in cache
roles can swap). Send most context to one model only
tune the delegate to report back by reference (file paths, high-level thinking), not by dump. For detection beyond heuristics, use internal-state probes (hallucination/lostness scoring)

token-burst heuristics are unproven ("we have to be very empirical to actually know"). Mine production signals — user model upgrades/downgrades, detected mis-routes — as a label stream and iterate the router against real usage. For prompts, prefer heavyweight smart-model repair (ask the model why it chose wrong, patch the prompt, rerun as regression) over gradient-style prompt tuning (GEPA-class)
data.name: Route sessions, not prompts — and keep a frontier watcher

guidelines: One failure has many candidate repairs (worked example: agent cites a stale policy and skips escalation — could be a stale memory fact, an unoptimized prompt, a tool that doesn't normalize the policy, a missing workflow escalation gate, or a weak-reasoning model)
do root-cause analysis and take the smallest durable change: memory writes (facts, distilled skills) cheapest/fastest → prompt/harness edits medium → weight updates (SFT/RL/LoRA) most expensive
score the fix before/after and run regression tests before shipping
data.name: Route each fix to the layer that explains the failure

guidelines: Not all traffic is equal — sending everything to the latest Opus-class model is a huge miss
define frontier-vs-everyday for YOUR product
For moderate tasks, assess open weights first without RL, on your own evals (your tool errors, your actual latency) rather than external benchmarks
Push deterministic work to CPUs — no LLM for CSV→PDF, CLI tool calls, or SQL
Layer governance on top: visibility into who uses what data, maintainability, control — model optionality is also a governance offering to customers
data.name: Route traffic by complexity; be the expert on what complexity is

guidelines: Write it before staffing engineers onto the project: (1) domain context + novel data representations (parti diagrams, circulation graphs, embeddings/latent spaces — "picture the software engineer we just hired from JP Morgan")
(2) business goal — why solving this matters
(3) type contract between core and ML repos and how types stay in sync
(4) persistence mapping — researchers should NOT go deep here, just map how far they got (a natural first entry point for engineering help)
(5) system anatomy — workflow vs. chained workflows, external LLM calls, model weights pulled in CI/CD
(6) merge/decomposition plan
data.name: Require an RPT document from every research prototype

guidelines: Make hierarchy levels real entity types with scoped context and their own approval boundaries
flow context down in slices, results up, and review only the top
force delegation: give orchestrators a CLI harness + skills where dispatching is the only path, or they'll do the work themselves
route every plan through one blocking review gateway (approve → hook fires the work); host it on an always-on machine, never a laptop that sleeps
collapse per-machine inboxes into one main gateway
add a single router (e.g., one Discord bot per machine) so the fleet is drivable from a phone
data.name: Structure an agent fleet as an org, not a flat pile

guidelines: Define the job in markdown (objective, target repo, metrics, hard constraints)
generate a baseline eval run + report first
one hypothesis per iteration, each on a fresh branch, one problem class at a time
run evals, write reports.md, update a global cross-run memory file
continue from improving branches, roll back regressions
explicitly forbid editing golden data/scorers to pass
cap iterations
review promising-but-failed hypotheses by hand and re-steer the next run
data.name: Run an AutoAgent-style self-optimization safely

guidelines: Wrap the agent you already have — point the simulation SDK at it, no code changes — and decide which tools have to be mocked for the run to be meaningful
drive the simulation with three inputs: personas, use cases, and the data points you want covered

for each persona generate the grounding data the agent will actually look up (identity, address, payment instrument, account state) and hold it consistent across every mocked tool call in the trajectory, or the run is not evaluable
give personas tone and voice as well as intent, so conversation style varies the way real traffic does
run judges per turn over the resulting conversations, and pipe the labelled dataset straight into the existing eval pipeline rather than building a parallel one
data.name: Manufacture agent eval data with simulations

guidelines: Assume goals will expand (helpfulness, confusion, injection) and that the needed access changes at runtime
never rely on the model or a single vendor's harness for safety — design for many models (including open ones) and many harnesses
run the agent inside an untrusted VM boundary with controls outside it
inject credentials as stubs so the agent never holds real secrets, and apply network policy and MCP control at the boundary

instead of one sandbox accreting capabilities, break work into tasks across security boundaries and run each in a scoped sub-sandbox with just-in-time tools composed over existing MCP tools but restricted to the task
decide additional access from the user's or task's intent at a control layer, denying or escalating what the intent doesn't justify
make the runtime follow the work — the same sandbox and policies locally, in the cloud, in your or the customer's VPC — and use that portability for fan-out and orchestration
data.name: Contain, scope, judge — independent of model and harness

guidelines: Don't build multi-agent orchestration until a single agentic loop is solid — start with one master agent that progressively loads skills
treat skills as the unit of context (context + tool execution), composed dynamically, tested and reused independently, with progressive disclosure
use a managed agent runtime but expect to fill gaps (session persistence, rehydration) yourself
replace logs with hook-based tracing at pre/post tool and decision points, emitting goal, reasons, belief status and confidence, so you can see where a 30-step agent got stuck
evaluate with trajectory evals (distance toward the goal) and treat inferred answers as regression signals routed to a human
put guardrails and fine-grained authorization at pre/post-tool hooks because agents act on behalf of users
reserve A2A for team boundaries
and budget for the two unsolved layers — cost and replay/debugging
data.name: Build the single loop first, then layer the reference architecture

guidelines: Judge every agent step by cost reduction or patient experience
treat X12 as the contract and reduce phone, portal and FHIR interactions to X12-like internal transactions with public, grounded schemas
map the full claim lifecycle (eligibility → attachments → submission → 999 → status → 835) and decide per step what is free reasoning and what is hard-coded
keep multimodal evidence in context rather than reducing images to conclusions too early
treat every payer answer as correct until evidence proves otherwise, expect contradictions between channels, and learn payer reliability
keep memory in-database, logically separated by partner, organization and user, and let users override it
re-validate before swapping in a newer model
and never run routine, high-volume steps on the most expensive model
data.name: Normalize to the standard, hold payer facts provisionally, balance and budget

guidelines: Decide explicitly what your review process is *for* — if it exists to grow trusted contributors (the Zig position), AI-assisted contributions break it and a ban is coherent

if it exists to absorb code, expect DDoS-scale AI bug reports and slop PRs and budget triage accordingly (curl's bug-bounty crisis). Blunt instruments are now legitimate: auto-close all PRs (tldraw), platform-level third-party-PR disabling (GitHub). Assume the community layer no longer verifies itself
treat every inbound contribution as unverified generation, and weigh whether cultivating contributors still pays when software itself is cheap
data.name: Choose a contribution policy before the slop chooses one for you

guidelines: Choose a target whose evaluation is fast and scalar (a five-minute training run's bits-per-byte, wall-clock seconds, kernel throughput) so the loop can run thousands of times
structure the system as the three-step scientific loop — ideation → implementation → validation — which holds across essentially every scientific field
give it retrieval/web search so it can find the competing ideas it has to beat
budget days rather than hours (all three published wins landed in one to a few days)
verify wins with the metric's owner (Recursive worked with NVIDIA on the kernel results) specifically to rule out reward hacking

and judge success by whether the system produced novel mechanisms rather than tuned hyperparameters — hash bi-gram/tri-gram embedding tables mixed into attention value paths through learned gates is the example of what a real find looks like
data.name: Pick targets where the metric is dense, cheap and hard to fake

guidelines: Put every surface — GitHub, Phabricator, and the agent loop — behind one review service that takes requests, ingests feedback and routes

run several generators at different cost/performance points (per-file logic checks, per-monorepo deep multi-file review with style guides and anti-patterns baked in, few-shot AI linters with deterministic context, custom team agents on knowledge bases and past PRs) and plug in third-party reviewers to benchmark against
post-process — rate, categorize, filter, deduplicate — so only high-confidence actionable comments reach anyone
instrument beyond cost and NPS: classify developer reply sentiment, track address rate per comment and per rule, profile agent trajectories to see wasted turns
assume the model is confidently wrong and add guardrails on what not to spend time on within the review time budget
route by risk profile and complexity, and keep security and compliance review centrally guaranteed
co-locate team customizations with the code through the ownership model and push each rule's address rate and sentiment back to its author
expect skill-writing to be trivial and skill-running at scale to be the work
raise the accuracy bar for agent consumers to avoid cavitation, and let agents absorb the nits
and as auto-approval arrives, move human review up to architecture, domain and product rather than removing it — its feedback is what trained the system
data.name: One review service, many generators, observability back to the rule owners

guidelines: Treat every task as code entering a pipeline: pin all dependencies, check the base image, catch missing fixtures, run the oracle solution and require it to pass (if you don't maintain an oracle, at least verify the verifiers fail when they should), run several real agent attempts to confirm the task is solvable *and* hard, tag difficulty (simple/medium/hard) by how often the agent succeeds, then explicitly approve it into the suite
For coverage, think integration test: bread-and-butter happy paths covering every main use case, plus edge cases (tool failures, database problems)
Keep a held-out split the agent's configuration was never iterated against — classic ML discipline, roughly 80/20 depending on the use case — so config tuning can't overfit the suite
Then iterate: establish a baseline, run the evaluation set, find failures, change exactly one thing, re-run, and re-run the full experiment before releasing
data.name: Run the benchmark through CI, and design its coverage

guidelines: Treat evals as a team sport: S&O set the quality bar, product writes rubrics, ops annotate, engineering provides APIs, telemetry, datasets and judges
run the loop continuously — capture traces and sessions, sample to a reviewable set, annotate with domain expertise, review, build golden datasets, calibrate judges against them, monitor, repeat
build the platform API-first on stable table APIs so engineers aren't blocked, then workflow-first so operators run it themselves
let operators vibe-code their own annotation UIs with coding agents instead of building one per use case
make judge calibration self-serve (baseline → GEPA optimization → promote) with any model and show the prompt diff so partners trust the result
and let each team choose who owns the judge prompt
data.name: Trace, sample, annotate, calibrate — with every function owning a step

guidelines: Refuse professional-services engagements even when profitable — they do not improve the product and do not scale. Require an outcome/ROI story from the beginning that chains to core business goals (every change getting AI review, QA and security analysis is ~87% less likely to hit a bug, so bug rate down X, customer satisfaction up Y, revenue/growth), which needs both engineering and business knowledge. Make the product self-assemble into the customer environment

manual install does not survive enterprise scale. Teach the model: hand the customer an autonomy roadmap they do not have, prove it in a couple of places, then let their team scale it. Route everything learned in the field back into the product surface — enterprise controls, harness quality, workflows, observability, cost controls, model routing are all improvement opportunities discovered in diverse orgs. Hire former founders, fluent technical communicators with executive presence, and systems thinkers who like closing loops
data.name: Run deployed engineering as the tip of the spear, not a services arm

guidelines: Locate your situation on two axes before choosing a method — how online your traces are (a one-time dump, a daily batch, or a live serving loop) and where your hints come from (static behavioural priors versus guidance constructed from the rollout just observed) — because the four combinations have genuinely different requirements and pay-offs
start in the offline-trace, offline-hint quadrant if you have nothing but logs, since it needs no replayable environment and can still install targeted behaviour changes
do not assume golden answers, as most real tasks have no per-task rubric — encode what good looks like as a behavioural prior instead

when you need broad improvement rather than one targeted behaviour, move to online hints constructed from each rollout, which adapt to whatever the model actually did and in measured comparison outperform applying one static hint to every rollout by a wide margin
cheat toward on-policy where you can — replaying an offline trace and rolling out a single on-policy step before hinting measurably beats the fully offline setup at almost no infrastructure cost
use a judge to pick where in the rollout to inject the hint and distil on the next step or few rather than the whole trajectory, since the KL learning signal decays with distance from the hint

mask irrelevant tokens with an LLM judge so you learn the behaviour rather than the teacher's connector-word habits, which improves out-of-distribution learning while limiting catastrophic degradation

and always track a non-regression metric alongside your target behaviour, since format rewards and naive SFT both degrade base capability in exactly the cases where the target behaviour is most out of distribution
data.name: Run enterprise distillation from production traces

guidelines: Build an internal benchmark before building any product and test it against what you have seen in the wild
roll out in stages — trusted alpha clinicians, beta, A/B at scale — and never stop monitoring
embed domain experts and have them write the judges so everyone else can hill-climb

where verification is as hard as generation, do not rely on one judge — combine quality, safety, adversarial and style judges, and ground the quality judge in rubrics written by two independent experts, adjudicated by a third and QA'd by a fourth
collect online signals (edits, thumbs, ratings)
decompose the workflow and post-train small models for subtasks whose quality is maxed, reserving the frontier for the rest, and invest in training where your data and focus can outpace the frontier
and use cheap gates to decide when heavy models run in live contexts
data.name: Benchmarks first, staged contact with reality, adjudicated rubrics, small models where quality is maxed

guidelines: Do product and distribution both
treat go-to-market as a data problem and build a live model of your world — classify the whole addressable market with semantic search, keep per-account data, alert on significant customer events
put every internal and external source behind a programmatic interface (MCP, CLI) so agents can act
give the GTM team many agents with internal data access and train them to use the tools well
keep consistent GUIs for repeated use cases alongside flexible chat agents
choose systems by arbitrary customizability rather than buy-vs-build, keeping SaaS that exposes MCP
consider capturing leadership judgement as evals for a draft-only clone with scoped tools
and staff a small forward-deployed engineering group that runs deals and builds the sales systems
data.name: Model the world, expose everything programmatically, keep only what agents can customize

guidelines: Before any loop: write down and encode your specs (desired architecture and architectural constraints, coding standards and acceptable patterns, dependency allow/deny lists, syntax standards, logging/observability/tracing practices) and your quality criteria (acceptable security/quality/maintainability levels — ship-with defaults exist, adjust per org). *Guide*: give the agent scoped context and guardrails for the task at hand — never the whole codebase, which produces thrashing, exploring and token burn. *Verify*: in the inner loop, have the agent call verification in real time and fix findings immediately so they don't propagate into later loops

in the outer loop, run LLM-driven and computational review together, grade the PR across quality/security/maintainability, and hard-gate merges on a passing grade. *Solve*: give the agent the tools and the agency to remediate its own findings, then repeat the loop. Keep verification multi-layered and reasoning-based, spanning quality, security and compliance
data.name: Run agentic coding as guide → verify → solve, in both loops

guidelines: Invest heavily in metrics before anything else — do not trust GPU-utilization (it reads 100% while under-utilized)

use tensor-core utilization as the real efficiency proxy, pull any GPU over ~78°C immediately rather than debugging it, and build custom exporters for InfiniBand and NVLink (wait times, errors, packets) because NVIDIA doesn't export them and most multi-node failures are cross-node communication

expect constant, often silent crashes (NCCL timeouts with green metrics) and let it crash rather than node-swapping — the same machines often run fine for 12–24h after — while checkpointing aggressively (every 20–30 min) on a fast trusted filesystem, not Ceph

share one cluster between training and production with a gang-scheduling queue that gives training strict priority, evicting inference and flipping it to another cluster or rented GPUs via virtual-kubelet, using taints to reserve/free in-cluster GPUs and a descheduler (not no-execute) to migrate production back slowly so it never drops
run low-priority diffusion inference on the worst, cheapest, most-preemptible GPUs since it tolerates bad hardware
and hide all of this from researchers so they just submit jobs
data.name: Run large-scale training on a shared cluster

guidelines: Score any post-training method against four axes before adopting it — is the task distribution online, is sampling on-policy, how much parallelism does it force, and is the reward per-token or per-sequence — since most methods trade two of these for the others
build the teacher by giving the *same* model privileged information rather than reaching for a larger one, so the technique still applies at the frontier

design hints as what the model should reasonably have known, not as the answer, and use an LLM pass to rewrite leaky hints (turn "the SSO token is expired" into "look through the logs"), because a hint the student could never have derived teaches it to skip reasoning and back-fill a justification

where you need a principled control, run a partial hint alongside the full hint and train against a linear combination, which measures how far out of distribution the guidance is and keeps the student from being pushed somewhere it has no overlap

expect long-horizon tool-calling to break naive implementations into hedging — watch for *wait*, *but* and *maybe* taking over your token distribution — and fix it by computing per-step KL divergence and applying it as a multiplicative token weight rather than a penalty, so diverged steps are down-weighted while recoveries still teach
and be honest that eval variance, format drift on tool calls and run-to-run instability all appear between the short-horizon regime where papers stop and the 100-tool-call regime where products live
data.name: Run on-policy self-distillation without leaking the answer

guidelines: Treat git worktrees as the isolation primitive — one folder per task so parallel sub-agents never contend over the same files — and drive them from the backlog you already have: every QA-reported bug ticket becomes a worktree with its own agent, which spawns its own sub-agents
don't queue the work yourself
the agent sequences better than you do

let the pipeline run end to end: parse the requirement, do root-cause analysis by pulling traces and logs, write the tests first, implement, run local end-to-end tests, open the PR, merge after review, build the image, deploy to dev, promote to stage, hand back to QA
keep the human at intake and final validation and out of everything between

collapse the whole surface — services and pods, system logs, tickets, PRs, agent session — into one pane so orchestration costs no window switching, and measure yourself on how many times you turn your head to ship one change
data.name: One isolated worktree per ticket; human at the ends only

guidelines: Pick one agent system and one real production path, not all of them, and ask for the receipt
(1) What woke it up? — user message, webhook, timer, tool result, sub-agent or replay
name the trigger and its identity, or you cannot reason about deduplication, order or authorization
(2) What state did it inherit? — transcript, session state, memory snapshot, policy version, tool surface
the model only reasons over the working set the harness assembled
(3) Which authority did it use? — actor, session, tool, run, arguments, scope, lifetime
